body: You thought the 2010s were wild? This decade is only a few years old, yet we’ve still never seen anything like this rapid pace of change and influx of interest. How? Why did it all come together in 2020? Perhaps that explanation starts how the decade began, with a debilitating global pandemic. But this is actually the end of the explanation, the final chapter. Refer to the previous 9 chapters of this Timeline and over 900 moments that describe and explain the technological and artistic developments that have led us here, from our earliest explorations of systems-based art-making to how digital technology and mass media art accelerated these developments in conjuncture with our digitizing lives.
For more context, we suggest [watching or listening (transcript) to our Ch 10 Artist Discussion with Lauren Lee McCarthy, Snowfro, Ix Shells and Rafael Lozano-Hemmer.]

But this 70,000-year story always had a twist coming at the end. Decades of advancements in computer science and AI research combined with our inexhaustible human capacity to intervene, experiment and create with emerging technologies led to a decade poised for disruption. Then, almost as soon as the decade began, a global pandemic hit. Increased time at home and stimulus liquidity fanned the embers we covered in chapters 1 through 9, igniting an NFT-mania.

This sudden and new-found popularity for digital, on-chain and generative art would have seemed unimaginable for people who had been working in these fields for decades in relative obscurity. These quiet builders have now become the heroes of this story, which is by no means winding down with this chapter. Paradoxically, unlike a traditional narrative, this story doesn’t end here and may only be beginning. Erick Calderon, a particular hero of this chapter, told the Le Random team more about the pandemic’s impact on “2020s: Digital Art’s Normalization.”

“For the last couple decades, we’ve seen this inevitable shift towards a more digital-focused world. We spend more of our lives online. And as a result, we value our digital possessions more than we did in the past. That’s something that was coming for a really long time.

The pandemic just helped everyone get there, or at least for me personally. It was pre-pandemic, post-pandemic in terms of how I crossed that chasm of understanding how much our time in the digital space impacts and affects us as humans, psychologically, emotionally, all those things.”
Seth Goldstein from Bright Moments also explained to me the impact of the pandemic:

“It’s not an accident that we started after the pandemic. The pandemic was a really raw time where we were all alone making stuff behind our computers. Bright Moments didn’t have any legacy business to support. We didn’t have existing galleries. We just saw the opportunity to bring people together.”

body: In July, Rafael Lima won a Tezos hackathon for a micro-funding project titled Hicetnunc. The grant was meant to fund a project “geared towards users in the e-sports community that [would] allow them to take part in crowdfunding.” By November of 2020, it would pivot again, “evolv[ing] into a tool for creating micro-funding DAOs for any purpose,” according to this interview with Lima. In the interview, Lima goes on to mention that future plans make include “Crypto art” and “NFT stores.”

The interview also explains the origin of the name Hicetnunc, inspired by existential philosophy from readings of Paul Virilio. Lima elucidated: “It concerns an existential praxis, a structure in perceiving references and making decisions upon them.” The following year saw Hicetnunc deploy on Tezos, kicking off NFTs on the platform in earnest and starting a surprising global digital art revolution that was particularly impactful and led by artists in the Global South, including Brazilian Lima.

body: Scheduled to be held in the middle of the pandemic, Rare Art Festival (RareAF) transitioned to a fully virtual experience, VRAF. The festival showcased a diverse range of art forms within platforms like Cryptovoxels. With over 50 live-streamed presentations, including by Kate Vass and Fanny Lakoubay, and numerous exhibits, VRAF did a noble job of carrying on through challenging times. The challenge was not only the pandemic. A huge issue for the still growing ecosystem, extending well into 2020, was a tepid secondary market. Growing the space was of prime concern in days that must have felt quite bleak, despite a recovery in the crypto markets following a catastrophic March 2020 crash. The event reminds us of the resiliency and determination necessary to survive in this space, as in one year the mood would be quite the opposite. At least two large catalysts for growth unexpectedly appeared later in 2020: October’s launch of NBA Top Shot and November’s Art Blocks. The stage was set for one of the wildest and unexpected years in this story: 2021.

Earlier in the year at the VRAF, a huge challenge discussed was how to onboard new people interested in the possibilities enabled by NFTs for digital art. In February of 2020, Decentraland launched, which joined CryptoVoxels as an early interpretation of the metaverse. Decentraland would play a critical role in onboarding big brands and celebrities in the coming months and years, eager to buy the virtual real estate. The second onboarding surge came from NBA Top Shot, which was meant to capture ownable basketball highlights for fans to collect and trade but quickly turned into a speculative frenzy with the seeming ease at which you could make quick money. Top Shot introduced a large new crowd to NFTs—and they had capital.

body: While founded in 2018 by Duncan and Griffin Cock Foster and acquired in 2019 by Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss, Nifty Gateway accounted for much of the 2020 NFT sales. Originally meant to mass-onboard users to NFTs by introducing credit card purchases and branding them as “nifties,” Nifty Gateway played a significant role in fueling the early NFT craze in early 2021, where “Nifty Gateway accounted for $75 million of the $91 million in NFT art auctioned in February 2021,” according to data by CryptoArt.io on Forbes.

Further, Nifty Gateway onboarded Beeple to NFTs and was responsible for his rapid rise in fame through a series of drops in 2020 that propelled his future astronomical prices. The platform also helped popularize other crypto-native artists like Pak, Refik Anadol, Sam Spratt and XCOPY.

body: Along with platforms like Nifty Gateway, prior to the major NFT-led digital art mania of 2021, early DAOs such as Flamingo (October 2020) began emerging with the goal of securing on-chain digital culture through a decentralized ownership structure. Fingerprints DAO and Pleasr DAO sprung up in March 2021, while GrailersDAO began in October 2021. These DAOs not only built some of the most significant blockchain art collections, they also pioneered a novel form of decentralized communal art collecting and, ultimately, curating. Much of this story over ten chapters has been about access to art (and technology) with examples extending at least to GRAV’s efforts to bring art to the public. Revolutions in access for artists and audiences occurred decades prior but DAOs democratize and globalize access to world-class art, finally revolutionizing collector access. This decentralized asset ownership structure has also served to foster a new generation of art collector demanding the conveniences afforded of the Internet—instant transactions and instant transfer.

body: Art Blocks Brings Generative Art On Chain

If NFTs unlocked demand, then Art Blocks, founded by Erick “Snowfro” Calderon, provided a space for demand to meet supply, creating a community where artists could manifest the technological, artistic and conceptual advancements of human history to push boundaries in art. The three genesis projects were released on November 27, including Jeff Davis’s Construction Token, DCA’s (Daniel Calderon Arenas) Genesis and Snowfro’s Chromie Squiggle.
Often credited with (re)launching generative art, Art Blocks was instrumental in introducing a wider audience to generative practice, especially on-chain long-form generative art.

These on-chain long-form generative art roots can be traced to earlier experimentation with systems, chance and community. Art Blocks Founder Calderon was a claimer and admirer of Larva Labs’ CryptoPunks. “As a generative artist, I thought CryptoPunks were a brilliant example of generative art,” Calderon told ArtNews. He arrived at the concept “from the day I claimed my CryptoPunks in 2017,” he told The Monty Report.
After years of exploring generative art and coding, Calderon envisioned a platform where artists could upload algorithms and mint unique, blockchain-verified art pieces in the vein of CryptoPunks.

Despite the influence of CryptoPunks, Art Blocks did not even have an NFT component until 2019. It also struggled to get off the ground in the early days. Calderon continued to The Monty Report: “I hit a wall in 2018 and early 2019, where I was like, ‘okay, yeah, Art Blocks isn’t going anywhere. I can’t communicate my vision. Nobody really wants to use this.’”
It was then that Calderon switched focus from pitching Art Blocks to helping the broader space grow. He began integrating himself into and understanding the tiny ecosystem he was looking to disrupt.

Despite these early setbacks, the platform’s auspicious November launch anticipated trends like few others. And no one, even founder Calderon, saw the enthusiasm that ensued coming, which he told to Le Random when reflecting on the 2020s.
Art Blocks genuinely redefined generative art with its focus on long-form and the NFT space early on in this decade, with the platform still a force in the space today.

body: Years in the making, the Art Blocks genesis project’s first iterations appeared on Twitter in September 2018 over two years before its official release on November 27, 2020.

Chromie Squiggle—affectionately referred to as Squiggles—is the art project Calderon developed around his years-long pursuit of the project Art Blocks. Squiggles played a key role in Art Blocks’s development, as Calderon would walk around in 2019 with a Chromie Squiggle card to help explain the concept of generative minting. “I handed them to different people and was trying to tell them the story, and they were looking at me with their eyes crossed,” Calderon told The Monty Report.
Today, the project is one of the most identifiable in all of generative art due to its recency and popularity in the broader NFT and crypto communities. Calderon writes humbly about the collection:
“Simple and easily identifiable, each squiggle embodies the soul of the Art Blocks platform. Consider each my personal signature as an artist, developer, and tinkerer.”

Davis has played a critical role this decade—and beyond—in creating and establishing generative art. His role became solidified when Davis released Construction Token, one of the three Art Blocks genesis projects. The other two were Chromie Squiggle by Erick Calderon (Snowfro) and Genesis by DCA (Daniel Calderon Arenas). The following year, Davis became an advisor to Bright Moments and the only artist to release work in each of its visited cities. His influence in the space remains as both an artist and as Chief Creative Officer and Strategic Advisor at Art Blocks.

body: This light sculpture on a flat plane above the viewer continued the two-decade career of the audio and light installation artists, teamLab, from Japan. Few groups have done more to popularize and normalize dynamic, code-based art to the public on a large scale than the influential teamLab with their nearly 400k subscribers on Instagram and the millions who have experienced their work live since 2001. Their work harkens back to the roots of electronic art and, therefore, to something fundamental to digital generative art: light and its manipulation.

body: This immersive, audiovisual exhibition was Fujimoto’s first solo show in North America, featuring over nine real-time, light-based installations powered by choreographed kinetic lasers, strobes, haze and moving lights. The work indicated a growing interest in immersive generative installations along with teamLab and Refik Anadol. The installations explored the universal connections between all living beings, revealing—as cybernetics did—the intricate and invisible systems that shape our reality. Set against a meditative soundscape inspired by the quiet of Shinto shrines, INTANGIBLE FORMS consists of hundreds of lasers algorithmically manipulated with the open-source toolkit openFrameworks to create the illusion of objects in space, harkening back to the roots of digital art—lumino-kinetic installation.

body: While perhaps not 2021 levels, 2020—the COVID year—still saw an overwhelming burst of digital creativity. Prior to the rise of long-form generative art the following year, most of these 2020 works would be considered short-form—or artist-curated—projects. The work we regard now may change over time, with some essential works certainly left out here. Yet code-based standouts of 2020 include: • cllm by Manolo: One of Manolo Gamboa Naon’s most striking works and his first mint on SuperRare • Limbo by Rebecca Allen (One of the luminary’s only NFTs and a work that visualizes her career, investigating form and repetition.) • RGB-2 series by Casey Reas • I’d rather be in a dark silence than and Anthropocene by Operator • Anticlassic, Loxodography 2 2, Petal Loops and Elektroanima by Tyler Hobbs (The palettes and developing aesthetic of his upcoming QQL and Fidenza can be glimpsed from these pre-NFT collections.)

body: This Lumen "BCS Immersive Environment Award Winner 2021” showcases Operator’s concept-forward explorations of systems. The piece—by the experiential artist duo of Ania Catherine and Dejha Ti—blends fashion, technology and experiential art in a postmodern, mixed media demonstration of the digital. The centerpiece is a signal-blocking trench coat, lined with military-grade fabric to protect against digital surveillance. Unveiled at Factory Berlin, the project placed participants in an immersive multisensory environment. It examines themes of data privacy and surveillance through 360° projections, soundscapes, AR filters and poetry. Operator’s work challenges the pervasive reach of surveillance technologies, offering provocative commentary on privacy in the digital age. Their work invites the viewer to consider the systems that run their lives, striking at.

body: We open January 2021 with a bang. This consequential deep learning model designed by OpenAI “generates”—as in creates—digital images from natural language descriptions. Utilizing a 12-billion parameter version of the GPT-3 neural network, DALL-E marked a significant advancement in AI-driven generativity. This launch opened the text-to-image race that continues today between DALL-E, Stable Diffusion and Midjourney. Although introduced at the very beginning of 2021, DALL-E and text-to-image generation did not receive mainstream attention until nearly a year later. This is because DALL-E 1 generated images autoregressively from discrete image tokens, which was computationally expensive and slow. It wasn’t until almost exactly a year later, in late December 2021, that the concept of latent diffusion models was introduced, which significantly reduced the computational requirements and decreased costs. This advancement would light the fire of mass adoption of the emerging technology.

body: Released on January 31st before NFT mania had properly taken hold, this iconic project would go on to be acquired by LACMA, sold at Sotheby’s and cemented in history as the crown jewel in one of the most notorious former collections. This Art Blocks Curated project stands as a massively significant part of a span that saw long-form generative art’s best-known releases, from Snowfro’s Chromie Squiggle in November 2020 through Tyler Hobbs’s Fidenza in June 2021. The collection helped establish the Canadian Cherniak as one of generative art’s rising superstars, propelling him to collaborations with MoMA on their postcards project and one of the most recognizable pieces in generative art: The Goose. While the project’s aesthetics on an individual level may not be universally considered innovative, the power of Ringers—and all generative systems—was in its ability to create a system that could produce 1,000 outputs. Taken as a whole, Ringers demonstrates, like Sol LeWitt and many others, the power of simplicity executed masterfully and thoughtfully.

Released on February 27, Golid’s Archetype was another early 2021 project that would later assume legendary status after a relatively quiet release on Art Blocks Curated. This long-form generative art project is rooted in the concept of rectangle partitioning. The algorithm divides and subdivides rectangles into intricate grids, creating varied compositions with six main properties: Framed, Shading, Scene, Palette, Coloring Strategy and Layout. With 600 minted pieces, Archetype shines in its display of the algorithm’s flexibility, producing consistently aesthetic works, from orderly grids to chaotic patterns.

img.credit: Kjetil Golid, Archetype #0, 2021. Art Blocks.

body: In February 2021, NFTs arrived on the Tezos blockchain, years in the making and just in time. Although perhaps some earlier NFTs were created as part of a November 2020 giveaway, the first Objkt.com-listed NFTs begin appearing in early February, including this piece, which may be the first Tezos NFT.
These early February pre-HEN-launch works include pieces by artists like Mario Klingemann, who minted work on Tezos in late February.

body: On March 1, Hicetnunc (HEN) officially launched its mainnet along with the OBJKT Swap Protocol on Tezos, which enabled NFT transactions. With low monetary barriers to entry and no gatekeepers, Hicetnunc exploded onto the digital art scene as a marketplace, fostering a loyal following of digital creatives from around the globe but particularly the Global South.

Before HEN, many established generative artists were skeptical of NFTs and avoided associations with them. As respected artists such as Mario Klingemann became some of the earliest adopters, HEN gained instant legitimacy. The platform rapidly became popular with a near-utopian, frenzied community. This explosion of creativity brought generative art from South America, with its illustrious legacy, to the entire world.
This author, Peter Bauman, wrote about critical moments throughout generative art history in South America on a collaboration with Bright Moments.

body: If two local catalysts propelled the NFT mania of 2021, they were the pandemic and this March 11 record-breaking Beeple sale. The macro-catalysts include the pre-conditions for NFTs that Casey Reas has spoken about and so much of this Timeline has been devoted to, including the rise of mass-media art in the ’80s, mobile technology and blockchains. Developments in systems thinking and abstraction throughout art history were also critical.

However, in terms of more proximate causes for NFT-mania, this sale did more than almost any single event to bring attention to NFTs and the art made on them. The traditional art world, while often appearing noble, is largely dictated by economics. This single—largely economic—event may have therefore done more for mainstream adoption of digital art than any other individual digital art effort in decades.
The flip side to the positive attention this sale may have brought to the space is the undoubted increase in financialization and speculation that it also ignited.
Art Blocks founder Erick Calderon spoke to Le Random about the challenges of hyperfinancialization in the decade.

body: Originally minted on Bitmark, Social Codes was a group online exhibition by Feral File and curated by artist Casey Reas in March before NFT-mania has properly taken off. The exhibition’s timing was perfect, as interest in the artists featured was rising rapidly. The ten artists included Dmitri Cherniak, LIA, Andrew Benson, LIA, Dmitri Cherniak, Raven Kwok, Anna Carreras, Manolo Gamboa Naon, Maya Man, Frederik Vanhoutte, Saskia Freeke and Dave Whyte (Bees and Bombs). Each artwork was created using custom software, and meant to showcase the power of code as a medium for artistic expression. Social Codes provided a cohesive space for these rapidly emerging digital artists to make work, curated by the legendary creator of Processsing itself. The show was thus a critical stamp of approval for some of the earliest generative art on the blockchain, increasingly, long-form generative art.

body: By April 23, when Matt DesLauriers released Subscapes, 2021-as-we-know-it was already taking shape with the Beeple sale, Art Blocks and HEN in the rearview mirror. Yet Subscapes on Art Blocks Curated was another generative art project that, in just a few month’s time, would reach legendary status. The hype for these early Art Blocks reached a peak a few months later, at the end of August, recording hundreds of ETH in volume per day. Comprising 650 unique on-chain iterations, each piece visualizes an otherworldly landscape inspired by topographic maps and hand drawn strokes. The outputs paradoxically appear at once natural, alien and mechanical, demonstrating DesLauriers’s mastery of his digital aesthetic.

After the dust settled in a chaotic generative art summer of 2021, Tyler Hobbs’s Fidenza in the end remains perhaps the most celebrated. This versatile and aesthetically diverse generative algorithm stood out for its recognizable elegance.

Rooted in the flow field algorithm for which the project is now nearly synonymous, Fidenza generates intricate, (mostly) non-overlapping curves that are layered with thick, curved rectangles, creating complex, organic compositions.

The algorithm allows for a wide range of variations in turbulence, scale, and color, producing outputs that range from serene, flowing patterns to bold, chaotic structures. Hobbs spoke to this author, Peter Bauman, about his evolving views on “algorithmic aesthetics”:
“This is the way I like to precisely define where the art is now: it’s the potential output space of the generative procedure combined with the curation model.

That is to say, I think what the artist has really crafted is that output space and all the things that can happen in it. Obviously, they don’t necessarily have control over exactly what happens but to a certain extent they do because they’re also able to choose the curation model.

For example, with Fidenza, I was developing it with the knowledge that every single output could be part of the final result set. That potential output space was designed with that curation model in mind—versus QQL, where I know that it’s going to undergo heavy curation, sometimes really extreme curation.

The algorithm can have a completely different type of output space and be successful and to ignore the curation model would be an oversight. So I think that’s where the art really lies but I think the results are probably the best way to judge the success of those other things—the tangible, observable effects. I think the art has already been, in some ways, created before those final outputs are even seen.”

In May, Bright Moments, co-founded by Seth Goldstein and Louie Ryan, began its journey. In a few short years, the ambitious organization traveled to ten—eight—cities around the world, organized a collection of 1,000 contemporary works and created a 10k NFT collection, CryptoCitizens.

The journey began at Bright Moments’ genesis location, Venice Beach, California. Starting as a community space for people to enjoy themselves around NFTs in person, Bright Moments from the beginning was able to incorporate a sense of playful seriousness into the physical appreciation of digital art.

The location also serves as the beginning of the community that Bright Moments would build over the course of the next few years, bringing many of the prominent names from this chapter together in places across the planet.

What Bright Moments in general and this event in particular signified was the increasing overlap of generative art, performance and real-life experience. Bright Moments made generative art something communal and experiential in a way it perhaps hadn’t been since Jasia Reichardt’s 1968 Cybernetic Serendipity or the early 1980s SIGGRAPH computer art fairs.

In December 2021, Bright Moments would travel to its first location outside of California with its New York event. The exhibition featured work by Tyler Hobbs and Emily Edelman, among others, signaling the beginnings of a rising global community.
Goldstein and Bright Moments artist and Art Blocks founder spoke to Le Random about the power of participation and community in art, fostered by Bright Moments.

In May, the self-taught coder Yard created the generative work Dreaming at Dusk for an NFT auction supporting the Tor Project. The artwork, derived from the private key of the first onion service, raised 500 ETH (approximately $2 million USD), marking a historic moment for both the artist and the organization. The work commemorates a piece of Internet history, harkening back to the days of net.art. The sale made Yard the highest-selling woman NFT artist on Foundation.

body: In June, Sotheby’s held its first-ever curated NFT auction, Natively Digital, marking a pivotal moment in the integration of digital art within the traditional art world. It’s no surprise that early forays from the art world came from the auction houses; however, museums like the Whitney and Buffalo AKG demonstrated interest in artistic interventions with blockchain technology years prior. This is thanks to the efforts of curators Christiane Paul and Tina Rivers Ryan, respectively. Perhaps a long-term disservice, the sale did muddle NFTs together as a “genre,” as co-curator and On NFTs author Robert Alice featured a diverse collection of 27 NFTs, including works from pioneering crypto artists and contemporary creators. The auction highlighted the historical breadth of digital ownership and scarcity, showcasing both historic NFTs and more contemporary digital art. Natively Digital solidified Sotheby’s role in this early NFT market and underscored the growing significance of blockchain-based art in the global art ecosystem. The sale was even flagged by artist Casey Reas as a critical moment. Despite these positives, leaning into the NFT aspect while being less sensitive to artistic practices and their potentially rich connective tissue remains a lost opportunity.

body: In July, the Institute of Contemporary Art in Miami (ICA Miami) acquired its first NFT, CryptoPunk 5293, as a gift from trustee Eduardo Burillo. The acquisition marks one of the very first by a museum anywhere, although the first was likely the Whitney several years earlier with Jennifer and Kevin McCoy’s Public Key / Private Key. Predating even this was MAK in Austria’s 2015 purchase with Bitcoin of the Harm van den Dorpel proto-NFT, Event Listeners.

Created by Larva Labs in 2017 and covered extensively in this chapter and the previous one, the acquisition further solidified the CryptoPunk series as culturally relevant. The acquisition marked a significant moment for the museum, highlighting its commitment to exploring contemporary art’s most emerging landscape. This early adoption of NFT art reflected an ongoing interest by ICA Miami to recognize the growing influence of blockchain technology in the art world.

body: Released as the so-called “Generative Art Summer” on Art Blocks was just beginning, the six-month stretch in the middle of 2021 marked a turning point. Interest and sales in generative art reached levels never seen before. What would have seemed unimaginable just a few months earlier peaked in late August 2021. CENTURY, a body of work Reas began in 2012, paid homage to 20th-century art movements, particularly inspired by Ellsworth Kelly’s 1950s works. Reas’s creation draws on concrete and non-objective art, color-field painting, and minimalism, the systems-thinking precursors to the Conceptual movement of the ’60s and ’70s that link directly to generative art’s history and are discussed in chapters 4 and 5. CENTURY as a series consisted of work that appeared to be “cut” and "reassembled” with viewer keyboard inputs, echoing Kelly’s practice of rearranging his paintings yet showcasing the ability of the digital to include interactivity. The collection is designed to be viewed on large screens and in motion, emphasizing its infinitely animating live code capabilities.

In September, Aaron Penne and Boreta released this infinitely generative audiovisual artwork with Bright Moments. The project is designed to evolve over 9 million years, combining randomized processes with meditative soundscapes and visuals. The work generates unique harmonies and patterns that continually shift over time. In 2022, it won the Lumen Prize NFT Award, as the project consisted of 1,000 unique NFTs, with the first 200 minted live at Bright Moments Gallery in Venice, CA, that September. This live minting event was one of the first by Bright Moments to capture what would become its raison d'être: the ability to connect collectors and artists in a deeply personal experience, blending digital and physical spaces and permanently linking the artwork to the moment of its creation on the blockchain but also in physical space and time.

In October, Facebook rebranded as Meta, signaling its strategic shift toward building a private metaverse—a virtual world blending social experiences, augmented reality and immersive environments. The moments is significant for this Timeline because it signifies that we are likely not even at the beginning in terms of people realizing the importance of digital ownership. When virtual reality becomes increasingly mixed with our physical reality, it’s not a far logical jump to suspect we will want these worlds customized to our specific aesthetic preferences, including the display of art work. Whether this company achieves its vision of a metaverse is unclear or even questionable, despite the fact that it’s extremely well capitalized and rich with personal data. The moment, however, signifies a step in the direction towards reality in what previous decades felt like science fiction. This particular announcement came at the Connect 2021 conference, where CEO Mark Zuckerberg outlined Meta’s vision to evolve beyond 2D screens, creating interconnected digital spaces where users can interact, work and play in new, immersive ways. This rebranding marked a significant transformation in the company’s focus, positioning Meta as a major player in any attempts to create a new virtual world. What that ultimately unlocks for digital fine art and its ownership suggests a bright future.

body: In late October, fxhash launched in beta. In early November, they released Project 0, FXHASH Generative Logo, the long-form generative art platform on Tezos’s genesis. Fxhash capitalized on the energy of NFTs, the vibrant Tezos art community, a pre-existing model in Art Blocks and a healthy dose of criticism from artists of the Ethereum blockchain. At this time in 2021, Ethereum was still PoW and came with significant environmental concerns attached. Its popularity also meant relatively extraordinarily high fees, which served to exclude artists from developing economies. From the beginning, fxhash aimed to provide artists with intuitive tools to create and sell their long-form generative art while offering collectors and curators a secure marketplace to explore and acquire these unique digital works. The platform quickly became a central hub for the generative art community, enabling global artists to earn a living from their creations and fostering a vibrant ecosystem. Fxhash’s launch marked a significant step forward in this story and the accessibility of software-based generativity. The first project—meant to be more of a proof of concept—and token minted on fxhash were created by ciphrd (Baptiste Crespy). FXHASH Generative Logo served as the platform’s logo, symbolizing the blockchain-enabled algorithmic process that generates unique outputs from individual hashes.

body: In October, Mario Klingemann launched Botto, a decentralized autonomous artist governed by a DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization). This decentralized autonomous artist was designed to generate and sell art based on community feedback mechanisms of the DAO.

Utilizing AI models and governed by the BottoDAO, Botto creates thousands of images weekly, with community members voting to select and auction the final artwork as NFTs. This project challenges traditional notions of authorship, harkening back to Harold Cohen and his AARON, which was similarly intended to be an immortal artist. While both AARON and Botto can operate somewhat independently of direct human control, Botto is guided instead by collective input and decentralized governance, meaning its future as a continuing artist is not limited by a single individual’s wishes or passing. The project’s roots lie in Gene Kogan’s Abraham.ai from 2017.

A few days after the platform’s official launch, fxhash founder ciphrd released the first collection proper: RGB Elementary Cellular Automaton (RBG). Inspired by Stephen Wolfram’s Elementary Cellular Automaton, the project is the quintessential study of a rule-based generative system. Recognizing the importance of this work, Le Random acquired RGB #1 from the artist himself.

In October, Asendorf released one of the projects for which he is most identified: Monogrid on HEN. This collection of 256 unique real-time animations was minted on Tezos with each 1/1 edition exploring the dance of density, color and motion within a grid of rectangles.

The series demonstrated Asendorf’s own “pixel sorting” technique, which he introduced as open source in 2012 and has significantly impacted the creating coding community. The process involves “separating a vertical or horizontal line of pixels in an image and sorting their positions into a different order” with shaders.

Monogrid evolves from low-density pixel grids to complex—mind bending—with animations dynamically altering the visual structure infinitely and in real time. This layered experiential work highlights Asendorf’s mastery of real-time generative art.

body: This October mid-career retrospective was co-produced by the Musée d’Art Contemporain de Montréal and SFMOMA. Unstable Presence displayed work from the decades-long career of Lozano-Hemmer. Known for his large-scale, participatory installations, the artist explores where technology, architecture and audience interaction meet. The exhibition featured a series of works that emphasized the transient nature of physical presence within natural and technological environments. By engaging viewers through interactive and performative installations, Unstable Presence, like much of Lozano-Hemmer’s work, highlights the poetic and political dimensions of our interactions with space, offering a unique commentary on the fluid nature of the ephemeral and the enduring.

body: In November, artist and AI educator Gene Kogan co-founded BrainDrops, a transformative NFT platform dedicated to AI-generated art. BrainDrops quickly became a central hub for artists and enthusiasts exploring the creative potential of AI. The platform launched in November 2021 with Kogan’s own Brain Loops; Roope Rainisto’s Life in West America, later its best-known release, followed in February 2023.
Kogan spoke to this author and Le Random for our talk, covering the previous decade.

BrainDrops continues to foster a vibrant community, offering educational resources and innovative tools, solidifying its role and strengthening the image of the much-derided AI-generated art in the eyes of the NFT and fine art worlds.

body: In November, a group of women poets established theVERSEverse NFT poetry gallery. The group celebrates poetry and text’s long-standing role in the history of generative expression, drawing from the legacies of artists like Hugo Ball, Christopher Strachey and Yoko Ono. The poets of theVERSEverse are Ana María Caballero, Sasha Stiles, Kalen Iwamoto and Elisabeth Sweet.

The gallery creates literary experiences that reimagine how we consume text-based creativity in a world increasingly confronted with zeros and ones. As this Timeline has referenced many times, text—with its set rules—has often predated visual aleatoric experimentation, a legacy theVERSEverse excitingly highlights.
Le Random is grateful that the poets have a strong connection to our Editorials and this Timeline.
Stiles is the only other co-author of this Timeline, writing dozens of the 1000+ moments.

Stiles also spoke to this author, Peter Bauman (Monk Antony) and Le Random’s Collection Lead Conrad House to discuss her digital poetry practice and the historical roots of generative text for Le Random Editorials.

Sweet has authored two articles on Le Random Editorials. The first was our fifth-ever piece, “Generations of Verse,” which examined the history of generative text. The second, “machine rêverie,” is a fantastic conversation with artist ‍aurèce vettier.
Ana María Caballero has contributed a piece to Le Random Editorials. When prompted to use an Editorial page as a blank canvas, she chose to share the details of her project, Paperwork.

On December 9, Michael Zancan released what would become one of fxhash’s most revered projects, Garden, Monoliths. Just examining this single day gives an indication of the burning flames of interest that were raging during this particular time period in generative art.

GM—as the project is affectionately known—is rooted in L-systems and based on the artist’s own “Grass.js” algorithm developed during a period of natural inspiration. The project features intricate vector-based designs that blend the density and organic patterns of nature with the rigidity of monolithic forms. Each artwork emerges as either a “Garden” or “Monolith,” representing variations of Zancan’s now signature style that combines delicate line strokes with occasional transparent fills, harkening back to the days of 1970s plotter artists experimenting with the organic. This includes the “grass” work of artists Colette and Charles J. Bangert as well as Grace C. Hertlein. This author, Peter Bauman, spoke to Colette Bangert about her naturalism-inspired work that would go on to deeply inform projects like GM, even if indirectly. Bangert said:
“There was always the changing sky, seasonal ground and what I saw in between as I looked, walked, traveled and lived.

Sometimes there were other people, other art. Mostly it was just me daily seeing and creating marks on a surface, then seeing what was there and once in a while that seeing went out into the world to be seen. The work itself, over the years, I named landscape as a way to understand and show connections to the world of the trees, sky, ground, green—or not look of the land—I’ve seen daily, even as the world climate changes everything. It’s colors, lines, forms and places daily, year by year, as I also change and grow onward.”

December 9 on fxhash alone saw the releases of Zancan, Erik Swahn’s Farbteiler, Loren Bednar, ge1doot, Michael Connolly (xiiixiii), Owen Moore, Rudxane’s Tych, collections by wblut, Loackme and many more. The period was simply an explosion of pent-up creativity that was finally released. For those lucky enough to be around the Discord chatrooms on days like this, there was an electricity and excitement that was never sustainable but demonstrated the potential of the space to move people.

In November, HEN founder Rafael Lima unexpectedly pulled the plug on the platform he created amid internal debate and pressure. Displaying the resiliency of decentralized Web3 organizations, HEN was quickly ported to alternative front-ends that were able to continue operations as usual. The resourcefulness and agility of the community is exemplified by Tezos members such as NftBiker, who started providing collecting and art tools, as part of a maturing ecosystem. This also saw the prominence of platform objkt.com increase. The community front-end Teia was formally launched in February 2022.

body: Co-founded by Timothy Mc Alister and launched as an NFT platform on the Tezos blockchain, objkt.com quickly becoming the largest digital art marketplace for NFTs on Tezos, akin to OpenSea on Ethereum. Initially starting as an auction site, it expanded into a full marketplace, especially after HEN’s usability challenges and instability following the departure of its founder. One of the earliest releases was a collaboration with artist and illustrator George Goodwin on the early Tezos PFP project Tezzards, helping to congeal the early Tezos art community. The platform played a pivotal role in shaping the Tezos art ecosystem, providing a decentralized space for artists and collectors to engage, mint, trade and showcase their work.

body: Unlike DALL-E, which generated images autoregressively from discrete image tokens, Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) operated in latent space and were the step that enabled text-to-image technology to go mainstream. Instead of working directly with pixels like Diffusion Models, LDMs first compress the image into a simpler, lower-dimensional space (called the latent space) using a pre-trained autoencoder. This compressed version of the image retains the essential information but is much less detailed. The diffusion model then works in this simpler space, which makes the process faster and less resource-intensive. Once the model has generated the image in the latent space, it’s converted back into a full, high-resolution image. Once this capability was introduced, text-to-image modeling became much less expensive and therefore widely available—and impactful.

This Lumen Global South Award Winner from 2021 is a generative art project that employs GANs to reimagine the lost bronze casting traditions of the Benin Kingdom, disrupted by the British invasion of 1897. Using datasets of looted ceremonial heads and other artifacts, Atairu creates AI-generated interpolations that explore the cultural and artistic absence inflicted by colonialism and its lasting scars. This mixed media collection also demonstrates the trend of how AI elements in art may eventually become ubiquitous. In addition to GANs, the work utilizes AR and 3D printing, reconstructing and reinterpreting these historical objects with the latest technology. IGÚN offers a dynamic vision that bridges past and present, while raising awareness of cultural restitution and historical memory. The project is a powerful demonstration of how systems thinking can be supplemented by AI to produce enduring artistic statements.

body: Centered on the history of shells as a medium of exchange, this standout AI project was created using a dataset of shells collected from the Thames in early 2021.

The project, comprising moving images generated by a GAN trained on these shells, reflects on themes of value, trade and the history of shells as one of humanity’s earliest forms of currency. The piece is not static, as the work is bought and sold, it evolves, expanding its dataset and altering its visual presentation. By training her own dataset, this work embeds the natural history of the Thames into the digital realm and the blockchain as only AI could. The difficulty, time and effort of projects like this also involve countless artist choices—yes, even for an AI work, Mr Chiang.

body: Honed over the course of several years through Takawo’s “dailycoding” practice beginning in 2015, Generativemasks features symmetrical geometric patterns that speak to generative art’s lush digital and material history. Alluding to the styles of indigenous Japanese culture, the collection highlights generative art’s ancient roots by one of its foremost contemporaries.

2021 saw a Big Bang-level outburst of work, creativity and pixels surely more than any other single year—although perhaps surpassed just the year later. 2021 was remarkable, a singular event in human history and time is needed to filter through the overwhelming level of outstanding works from the year. body: In the beginning of 2022, a nascent on-chain generative art community began to find its voice as organizations like Right Click Save, TENDER and Waiting To Be Signed joined Outland—first publishing November 30, 2021—in giving voice to artists and collectors with suddenly much to say. In 2021, these voices had been fairly insular, mostly kept to Art Blocks, fxhash and DAO Discord channels. Led by Editor-in-Chief Alex Estorick, Right Click Save is part of ClubNFT, which was founded by Jason Bailey (Artnome) and had artist Danielle King as its CFO. Together with Outland—led by Editor-in-Chief Brian Droitcour—they served as invaluable platforms for digital art’s written discourse in these critical early years.

body: In March, this generative long-form Art Blocks Curated project was inspired by traditional East Asian art and folklore. Through code, Xie recreates the fluidity and movement found in classical paintings, drawing inspiration from the colors and forms of woodblock prints.

The project evokes religious themes and mythological imagery—dragons, phoenixes and the qilin, a symbol of prosperity. Programmed in p5.js, Memories of Qilin merges ancient cultural heritage with modern digital techniques—a project typical of a day where the roles of religion and art are blurring.

body: While its beta debut was in late October 2021, April 2022 saw fxhash officially launch with version 1.0. The latest version greatly improved the user experience, including on a security level, overall platform upgrades and the ability to collaborate on a single contract. The upgrade was successful at eliminating many of the bugs of the beta version of fxhash, which included issues with unverified scam artist mints. The release brought fxhash out of its most feral, Wild West beginnings. Also critical to the early success of fxhash was the curatorial platform Tender, which cultivated early community voices such as Trinity and Will from podcast Waiting To Be Signed. Their careful effort cultivating serious discussion around work was an under-appreciated factor in the success of the early fxhash community.

body: In May, fxhash launched its first live minting event, Art Basel Hong Kong. The event was also one of the first public generative art minting experiences to engage the broader community as well as the traditional art world. With some of the top artists minting on fxhash at the time, the event was an earnest attempt to demonstrate the delights of minting a random work of generative art.
This author, Peter Bauman, went to the event in person and wrote this related piece shortly after on fxtext.

In May, the cryptocurrency market experienced one of its worst runs to date. It was caused by the sudden catastrophic collapse of the cryptocurrency and Web3 organization Terra, which included LUNA and stable coin UST. The event sent shockwaves through the entire Web3 community and portended a more muted period in the space after unprecedented levels of interest and hysteria in the previous 18 months. Central to this downfall were UST, Terra’s algorithmic stablecoin, and the Anchor protocol, which offered unsustainably high yields to attract deposits. As concerns over the stability of the system grew, a massive run on UST ensued, leading to the dramatic devaluation of Terra’s native token, LUNA. The implosion wiped out billions in value, exposing critical vulnerabilities in decentralized finance (DeFi) and raising questions about transparency and investor protection in the crypto space.

body: In June, Verse, founded by Jamie Gourlay and Augustinas Malinauskas, launched with the goal of bringing order and legitimacy to the chaotic NFT art market. Verse introduced a curated, elevated approach to NFT sales, led by former Tate Britain curator Leyla Fakhr and Creative Director Dr Mimi Nguyen. The platform’s first exhibition, This Is Tomorrow, featured works selected by a panel including Simon Denny and Tyler Hobbs. Verse describes its opening as the beginning of an aim “to encourage the collaboration between artists and curators, and create a space where artists can showcase works that may not have been ownable to collectors before NFTs.” Since its launch, Verse—along with Art Blocks, fxhash and others—helped shape a decade where creatives’ tools and access were expanded like never before.

body: In July, the auction house Phillips presented this respectable online auction, curated by Georg Bak, and exhibition tracing the evolution of generative art. The event featured works from early pioneers like Vera Molnar and Herbert W. Franke, alongside contemporary artists such as Snowfro and Dmitri Cherniak. The exhibition, which traveled from Paris to London, showcased the various connections between pioneers of computational art. The exhibition did well to highlight the rich history of generative art within both traditional and NFT markets at a time when this history was less well known.

body: In September, Tyler Hobbs and Dandelion Mané introduced their co-creative QQL, a collaborative generative art project, empowering collectors to curate their own unique pieces from the pair’s versatile algorithm.

The collection was novel in the way a highly successful artist was willing to experiment with a demonstration one of the core principles of generativity—cession of control but also authorship. The question of authorship extends ideas of groups such as GRAV who de-emphasized the individual creator, stressing collective creation.

The project itself consisted of 999 Mint Passes, holders of which could then mint their selected outputs. This allowed for hundreds of community members to contribute to a dynamic, evolving collection underscoring communal engagement.

The project anticipated the increased creative exploration of co-creation, which this author, Peter Bauman, wrote about for Right Click Save in early 2023. This shift included the launch of fxparams in March, 2023, which showed that the wider community was interested in exploring and embracing co-creative art.

In September, Ethereum released the Bellatrix upgrade to initiate “The Merge” process of transitioning from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake. The relevance of the Merge for this story is that many artists refused to engage with Ethereum previously due to its ecological impact in particular. This shift significantly reduced the network’s energy consumption by approximately 99%, addressing those growing concerns over the environmental impact of its technology. The Merge also aimed to enhance the network’s scalability and security by replacing energy-intensive mining with a system where validators stake their Ether to participate in block creation.

The exhibition showcased a broad spectrum of algorithmic art, from early generative works to modern AI-driven pieces, demonstrating the evolving role of machines in the creative process and the collaboration between artist-programmers and their digital tools since the ideas of Shannon, Bense and Moles.

body: In November, Refik Anadol unveiled Unsupervised at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), a groundbreaking AI-driven installation that reimagines over 200 years of the museum’s collection. Using a machine-learning model trained on MoMA’s publicly available data, Anadol’s work continuously generates new, immersive digital forms, reflecting the museum’s environment in real-time. Unsupervised explores the intersection of technology and creativity, offering viewers a visionary reinterpretation of modern art through a dynamic, ever-changing display. The installation is also tokenized on the blockchain, highlighting the integration of digital art within contemporary museum practices. The following year, the piece would be donated to the museum by 1OF1, led by Ryan Zurrer, with the RFC Collection, in an indication of the museum’s interest in emerging technologies.

body: In early April, Bright Moments held their first international event, renting Kraftwerk in Berlin for 10 nights of communal celebrating. A few months later in July, the team reassembled in London, marking the mid-way point in its journey thus far. In November, the production packed up and moved to Mexico City, which saw the anticipated release of 100 Untitled Spaces by Erick Calderon (Snowfro). These opportunies provided critical opportunities for both the existing community to meet and socialize, but also attracted newcomers to the space with its more laid and contemporary approach to a traveling art exhibition.

body: In November, as this author was attending the previously mentioned Bright Moments Mexico City, news began breaking of the collapse of the FTX crypto exchange and Alameda Research. Once one of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges, FTX precipitously collapsed in a matter of days, stunning the industry and giving a further black eye to anything related to crypto or NFTs. The downfall began when a report revealed the financial instability of Alameda Research, FTX’s sister company, leading to a market panic. Binance—the Chinese-based company considered FTX’s main rival—initially considered rescuing FTX but withdrew after reviewing its finances. FTX filed for bankruptcy on November 11, with CEO Sam Bankman-Fried resigning amid accusations of fraud. The collapse triggered a broader crisis in the cryptocurrency market, with FTX owing billions to creditors and sparking a major loss of confidence in the industry, the cloud of which remains to this writing.

body: In August, just a few weeks after the public release of Midjourney, Stability AI publicly released Stable Diffusion, a text-to-image model co-developed with researchers from LMU Munich and Runway ML. The release marked a the third significant text-to-image generative AI model in less than a year. Combined, these models played a significant role is expanding access to creative tools. Stable Diffusion in particular achieved this as the model operates on under an open-source license. As with the other generative AI tools released in this whirlwind period, within months, the model garnered over 10 million users, sparking both widespread interest, curiosity and fear in these emerging technologies.

body: In September, Lozano-Hemmer had his first solo exhibition at Pace since joining the gallery. Common Measures featured three major installations showcasing his use of digital technologies, including AI, robotics and projection mapping. Lozano-Hemmer’s poetic work utilizes software and systems to engage audiences in interactive experiences that explore social, political and scientific themes. This exhibition continued his exploration of the intersection between architecture and performance, drawing on traditions of public-facing work in the vein of GRAV, phantasmagoria and animatronics.

body: Sputniko!’s Menstrualverse challenges the representation of gender in virtual realities by introducing the artists’s famed Menstruation Machine (2010 and found on this Ttimeline) as a wearable avatar accessory in Decentraland. The wearable enabled users to publicly perform menstruation in the Metaverse so as not to transpose its taboo from physical to virtual worlds. Ironically, these attempts to expand gender expression, resulted in the wearable being rejected by Decentraland due to safety and age standards. Menstrualverse raises critical questions about identity, autonomy and the future of bodily performance in digital spaces, harkening back to the questions and ideas of artists such as Copper Giloth and Rebecca Allen. The work questions whether the Metaverse will reflect or erase biological realities—and their prejudiced taboos.

The foundation’s mission is to introduce and cultivate this computational art form through exhibitions and educational programs, fostering a broader engagement with contemporary digital creativity.

JGAF also aims to create opportunities for artists and build an international network dedicated to generative art, positioning itself as a pivotal force in promoting generativity globally. The project was funded by sales from Takawo’s Generativemasks.

body: In November, Buffalo AKG and Casey Reas’s Feral File presented the online exhibition Peer to Peer. The show served as a promising indication of the growing overlap between art associated with blockchain technology and major contemporary art institutions. The show, curated by Dr. Tina Rivers Ryan—now at Artforum—featured thirteen new works from global artists, utilizing AI, 3D modeling and smart contracts to reimagine themes from the museum’s collection. As the first American museum survey of blockchain art, it highlighted the emerging role of museums in a decentralized art world. Proceeds from the exhibition support the museum’s new media art gallery and digital technology lab, with works remaining accessible through Feral File. The show featured work of LaTurbo Avedon, Mitchell F. Chan, Entangled Others, Simon Denny, Amir H. Fallah, Sarah Friend, Auriea Harvey, Rhea Myers, Osinachi, Casey Reas, Anne Spalter, Itzel Yard (Ix Shells) and Sarah Zucker. The following year, the exhibition would again be in the news as all 16 of the works were acquired as NFTs by Buffalo AKG’s Dr. Ryan.

Curated by Dr. Tina Rivers Ryan, the exhibition highlighted global artists exploring blockchain technology, reinforcing the museum’s 160-year legacy of engaging with emerging artistic movements. The acquisition includes works by LaTurbo Avedon, Mitchell F. Chan, Entangled Others, Simon Denny, Amir H. body: In December, engineer Casey Rodarmor created Inscription 0 of the new Bitcoin protocol Ordinals. Within months, the community had grown significantly, especially as marketplaces like Imagine Art and Generative appeared in 2023. Ordinals reignited an apparently dormant interest in the possibilities of digital ownership—beyond currency—on Bitcoin. This reminds of the previous decade’s earliest NFT ideas, which featured essentially the only options available at the time: Bitcoin and its forks, like Namecoin. Bitcoin’s place in this history was secure before Ordinals, but certainly makes it even more relevant now. The reason: Bitcoin now had its own cultural artifacts, which, like NFTs or artifacts of any kind, varied in quality.

body: Unlike many of the previous exhibitions at major museums that celebrated art and technology, Coded did not go so far as to showcase any contemporary practitioners of code-based art; however, the show was instrumental in recontextualizing and legitimizing four decades of history in art and technology. Coded highlighted how artists from 1952 to 1982 harnessed early computing technology. The exhibition, featuring 100 works by pioneers like Vera Molnár, Frieder Nake and Stan VanDerBeek, institutionalizes the evolution of generative practices and digital systems aesthetics. This landmark showcase, curated with historical precision by Leslie Jones, illustrates the foundational role of algorithmic, systems thinking and programming in the history of art. Anne and Michael Spalter provided work for the show through their Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection. The show was also largely supported by digital art patrons Carl & Marilynn Thoma, whose Thoma Foundation funds nearly every major digital art exhitition in the United States. Ultimately, Coded provided much absent contextualization to a movement long overlooked, while signaling the upswing in digital art’s evolving relationship with institutions.

body: In January, following closely behind the heels of Buffalo AKG, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) acquired its first NFT just a few weeks after Buffalo’s acquisition. This embrace of the latest from the digital art movement was part of a global embrace of NFTs by modern art institutions around the world in 2023. The piece itself, Final Transformation #2 (2022) was by Lynn Hershman Leeson, known for her exploration of technology’s impact on humanity. The artist created the NFT as part of her ongoing engagement with digital media and film. The work featured an excerpt from her 1997 film Conceiving Ada and a nod to her installation Room #8 (2006–18). It was generously donated by the artist. This acquisition marks SFMOMA’s commitment to integrating digital innovation into its esteemed collection.

body: In March, OpenAI achieved a major advancement in artificial intelligence functionality and adoption. GPT-4’s enhanced reasoning, creativity and problem-solving abilities surpassed its predecessors. The model’s prominence and entrance into the social and creative milieu were dizzying. The large language model handles tasks like composing complex texts, interpreting images and interactive dialogue, showcasing a significant leap in AI capabilities that could be applied towards creative ends. While predictive text isn’t new (Google Translate 2006, Siri 2011, etc), the sophistication jump from these early examples to GPT4 caught all non-AI researchers off guard. A technology that for decades—since perhaps the ’60s—was thought to be right around the corner, 5 years away, suddenly was actually here. ChatGPT, which GPT-4 was folded into, reached 100 million users in 2 months, beating platforms like Instagram and TikTok by significant margins. Not without its drawbacks or critics, the technology and its peers nonetheless will shape the future of content and art for the foreseeable future.

In February, the Centre Pompidou became the first major institution outside of North America dedicated to modern and contemporary art to acquire a collection of NFTs. Just two months prior, Buffalo AKG acquired 16 works as NFTs from their online exhibition Peer to Peer. Nonetheless, the Pompidou’s acquisition must be considered historic and included works from thirteen artists, including Larva Labs—the CryptoPunks and Autoglyph creators Matt Hall and John Watkinson—Jonas Lund, Fred Forest and emerging figures such as aaajiao and Émilie Brout & Maxime Marion. The collection, consisting of eighteen projects, explored how blockchain technology and artistic creation could reinforce each other as well as the museum’s commitment to contemporary technological innovation. The acquisition highlighted the museum’s interest in the emerging technologies that expanded the definition of art in the digital age. Another major modern art museum would announce NFT acquisitions just three days later.

body: In February, just three days after Centre Pompidou’s NFT acquisition announcement, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) announced their own significant acquisition of NFTs. The move was a further indication of the growing acceptance of blockchain-based work in the world’s largest art institutions. This collection included a gift from prominent collector Cozomo de’ Medici featuring noteworthy new media artists such as Monica Rizzolli, Dmitri Cherniak, Justin Aversano, Cai Guo Qiang, Matt DesLauriers and Claire Silver. It also saw works enter through individual donations by John Gerrard and Tom Sachs’s Rocket Factory. Work by Erick Calderon also entered the collection in this bundle. The previous year, LACMA, in collaboration with of all people, Paris Hilton, launched a fund to acquire digital art by women, including works by Nancy Baker Cahill, Shantell Martin and Krista Kim. LACMA also partnered with Cactoid Labs to commission digital artists to create pieces inspired by the museum’s collection. This series featured works by Monica Rizzolli, Ix Shells, Jen Stark, Emily Xie, Sarah Zucker, 0xDEAFBEEF, William Mapan and Tyler Hobbs. The growing collection reflects LACMA’s lasting commitment to exploring new media and expanding its collection to include cutting-edge forms of artistic expression. The bundle acquisition underscores the growing recognition of blockchain-based art within the traditional art world, especially juxtaposed to the acquisitions by Buffalo AKG and Centre Pompidou.

body: This 2023 Lumen Prize Metaversal Generative Art Award Winner and Art Blocks Curated long-form generative art project fused code, choreography and cryptography into a visceral, three-act experience. This author, Peter Bauman, spoke to artist duo Operator’s Ania Catherine and Dejha Ti about the project in “Operator on Human Unreadable” at Le Random Editorials.

The work challenges the clean, universal aesthetics of modernism by introducing vulnerability, risk and the human body into the digital realm in the vein of pioneers like Analivia Cordeiro and Rebecca Allen. Each piece in the collection is driven by on-chain choreographic data, creating a dialogue between human expression and technical systems. Human Unreadable invites audiences to engage with the chaotic and embodied aspects of human experience, probing the possibilities of human-machine collaboration on the blockchain, while liberating the movement from the screen.
“As Conceptualism liberated the ’60s art world from the canvas. Operator’s Human Unreadable liberates the on-chain generative art world from the screen.” -Peter Bauman

In May and November of 2023, Bright Moments continued its global tour with vibrant events in Tokyo and Buenos Aires. In Tokyo, the experience included nightly minting at a skyscraper by Shibuya Crossing, personalized gallery tours in a traditional Japanese house, and a grand reveal at one of the city’s renowned nightclubs. The Le Random team of thefunnyguys and this author, Peter Bauman, spoke at the Tokyo event on ten moments from this very Timeline. The set the stage and context for the artist talks. Buenos Aires followed with equally immersive events, further solidifying Bright Moments' commitment to connecting digital spaces with real-world communities. Le Random’s thefunnyguys and Bauman spoke at this event as well, describing ten moments in generative art history from the South America and the world. These city-wide experiences not only showcased the unique cultural essence of each culturally iconic location but also strengthened the global generative art community through shared, in-person experiences, harkening back to the early-80s computer art community SIGGRAPH nurtured in North America or the similar organization a continent away in Ars Electronica. What made Bright Moments was that it was truly and intentionally a global endeavor.

In March, bitforms gallery in New York presented Code Chronicles, curated by Aleksandra Artamonovskaja now Head of Art at Tezos (Trilitech). This exhibition featured generative artworks by eight pioneering artists, demonstrating the links between on-chain generativity and its code-based predecessors. Artists included LIA, Sara Ludy, Ana Maria Caballero, Maya Man, Helena Sarin, Sarah Ridgley, Sarah Friend and Ivona Tau.
Listen to Le Random’s chat with LIA about beginning her career in the ’90s for our Timeline Ch 7 talk.

The show explored the intersection of digital identity, memory and generative processes, highlighting how these hyper-emerging technologies were impacting digital expression. Each piece emphasized the dynamic relationship between artist and algorithm, reflecting on themes of impermanence and the blurred distinctions between human creativity and machine intelligence. The show demonstrated a thoughtful link between the gallery world and artists exploring on-chain.

With the proliferation of generative AI tools in 2022 (DALL-E, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion), it’s not surprising to see platforms arise to service the growing field. These included Fellowship by Alejandro Cartegena, BrainDrops by Gene Kogan, Emergent Properties, K011 and SkaldaAI.
Cartegena, a photographer with work in SFMOMA, co-founded Fellowship in 2021 as an NFT photography platform, which since transitioned to an AI focus.

In December 2022, Johann König relaunched EXPANDED.ART—formerly Misa, which had been founded in July, 2021—as a physical gallery in Berlin and online marketplace. It focuses on integrating Web3 technology, contextualizing digital pioneers and supporting female and non-binary artists.
Another vibrant platform that’s appeared during this time is Highlight, co-founded by Nat Emodi, which affords artists several minting options and chains.

Around this time, Bitcoin Ordinals also began growing its community. This followed the first ordinal inscription, which took place in December 2022, kicking high levels of the possibilities of digital ownership beyond currency on Bitcoin. This reminds of the previous decade’s earliest NFT ideas, which featured essentially the only options available at the time: Bitcoin and its forks, like Namecoin. Bitcoin’s place in this history was secure before Ordinals, but certainly makes it even more relevant now. Two Ordinals platforms arose: Imagine Art and Generative.

Finally, several “Open Minting” platforms appeared around this time that aimed to enable creators with an ever-expanding suite of mixed-media digital tools. These platforms included the previously mentioned Highlight, which proved to be the most enduring. Others are Alba, EditArt, Mint256, Prohibition and Re-tain.
This interest in platform growth between 2022 and 2023 demonstrated the deep impact these emerging technologies had on a variety of new media practices and interventions.

body: In October, MoMA introduced the MoMA Postcard project, an enormous stamp of approval from a global modern art museum on the creative application of emerging technologies. The blockchain-based initiative encouraged global collaboration in digital art through the creation of free art works. The project began with 15 artists creating digital postcards, each evolving as it traveled across continents. This collective effort highlighted the potential of web3 technologies to foster co-creativity, community, and new forms of artistic expression. MoMA Postcard was an encouraging sign that major institutions would not take decades to begin taking these emergent art forms seriously. The participative element also highlighted blockchain art’s ability to engage globally in simple yet meaningful ways, emphasizing the accessibility and collaborative spirit at the core of the digital art movement.

body: In December, fxhash launched its long-awaited version 2.0, which incorporated Ethereum minting capabilities in addition to Tezos.
Fxhash founder ciphrd spoke to this author, Peter Bauman, about the launch. Also joining were Paul Schmidt and Charlie Middleton.

“We didn’t want to be positioned as a tool that opens up any creativity while limiting our artists in terms of reach because, well, some collectors only collect on Tezos or Ethereum. There is a crossover between those collector groups, but essentially, there are also a lot of differences between these blockchains. It’s in that regard that we wanted to integrate Ethereum into the platform.”

body: In December, the real-time generative art trio AGH, consisting of Kim Asendorf, Andreas Gysin and Leander Herzog, debuted their collective show, AGH 1, in Berlin, organized and co-curated by Grailers with support from Fingerprints and Highlight. The group, known for their shared focus on digital aesthetics and real-time code-based art, used this platform to challenge traditional art narratives and glorify the intrinsic beauty of computational processes.

Their work celebrates the digital, emphasizing its inherent qualities such as motion, interactivity and adaptability. They aim to create a new, responsive art form that reflects the technological possibilities of the contemporary digital age.
The three artists spoke to this author, Peter Bauman (Monk Antony) about the event for Le Random Editorials.

body: In December, the art world and, especially the generative and digital art communities, bid farewell to the Grande Dame, Vera Molnár, a pioneering figure in generative, systems and algorithmic art.
This author, Peter Bauman, wrote “Molnár’s Paris,” taking a look at the artist’s storied life spent mostly in the French capital.

Born in 1924, but moving to Paris in 1947 after WWII, the Hungarian artist was a trailblazer in merging human creativity with computational precision, coining the term and concept machine imaginaire to describe her innovative approach. Molnár’s work, spanning over six decades, explored the symbiosis between hand-drawn elements and algorithmic systems, with intense and prolonged interest, leaving a lasting mark on what the digital could achieve.

body: 2024 was a big year. It’s so hard to tell living through it; it’s hard to hear clearly in the din of noise. It was also a year of contrasts. It was the best of times, it was—you know. Let’s start with the good news—the age of wisdom, the epoch of belief, the season of Light. Digital art had a moment in 2024—actually it had several moments. The first was February to March. February saw the Pompidou, Whitney and MOMI all open major historical generative art exhibitions with shows on Vera Molnár, Harold Cohen and Auriea Harvey, respectively. Later in the month, MoMA announced a blockchain-based exhibition with Feral File that included artists like Yoko Ono and Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst—their names will come up again. Just a few weeks later, Tina Rivers Ryan—a renowned digital curator whose Electric Op also appears this year—announced she would be taking over as editor at Artforum, one of contemporary art’s premier publications. This came just after Taschen released its mammoth On NFTs book by Robert Alice studio during Bright Moments and NFT Paris. It was a big couple of months for media and digital art—a proper moment. It would have been the highlight of many prior years on this Timeline. But 2024 was only really getting started. Did I mention that Herndon and Dryhurst had big years? Besides the aforementioned MoMA show, they also participated in the Whitney Biennial and took over the entirety of Serpentine North for this author’s work of the year, The Call. By the middle of the year, we were treated to one of the year’s most unique events, the historic Generative Art Summit in Berlin that celebrated the form from its analog roots to its turn to digital computation. Organized by Dr. Susanne Paech from the HWF Foundation, the conference included some of the most impactful figures in generative art over the last sixty years: artists, thinkers, writers, gallerists, academics and curators. It won’t be possible to repeat the event in the same way beyond the logistical challenges due to the availability of the attendees moving forward. This author was lucky to be a part of it and speak on behalf of Le Random with Dr Paech and thefunnyguys. The second half of the year included more major exhibitions. First up were MUDAM’s Radical Software and Buffalo AKG’s Electric Op in September. November saw LACMA’s Digital Witness—part of Getty’s much larger art and technology themed event PST ART—and perhaps the event of the year, Tate’s Electric Dreams. Institutions like MoMA, Tate, Pompidou, LACMA, Whitney, Serpentine, Artforum and more demonstrated serious and impactful commitment and interest to digital art in 2024. Without question, this second half of the year was another moment. In fact, that’s exactly how Tina Rivers Ryan explained it to me in early 2025. Now for the not-so-great news—the age of foolishness, the epoch of incredulity, the season of Darkness. 2024 saw both the legacy and digital art worlds struggle in seeming coordination with museums laying off staff, commercial galleries closing and auction houses struggling. At the same time, the digital and Web3 world saw galleries close, marketplaces shutdown and free-minting platforms gain in popularity. Yet some marketplaces thrived in 2024, including Verse and Fellowship in particular, while Art Blocks, Highlight and fxhash completed partial pivots to continue their great work. 2024 was a Dickensian year—about the haves and have nots. The history books will and should remember it as a year of Light for digital art—certainly it had its moments as Tina Rivers Ryan described to me in early 2025. But for many, the lights turned out and perhaps for good. In the spirit of this Timeline’s broad perspective, 2024 was undoubtedly a momentous year. It was perhaps the year you could say with confidence that the digital, Web3 and legacy art worlds were as connected as ever.
Auriea Harvey’s My Veins Are the Wires, My Body Is Your Keyboard at Museum of the Moving Image presented a landmark survey of Harvey’s career, opening in February.

The exhibition was curated by Regina Harsanyi and explored Harvey’s oeuvre, dating back to her seminal early work in net art in the 1990s. It also included interactive media and digital sculpture, showcasing the depth of the artist’s career. Featuring archival material, interviews and newly commissioned works, the exhibition examined themes of digital materiality, intimacy and technological embodiment. It was accompanied by a publication with contributions from scholars and artists, reflecting on Harvey’s impact on digital and interactive art.
We spoke to Harvey for our Timeline chat on the 1990s.
The show also received extensive critical acclaim and served to introduce thousands to the work of a net art legend.

body: Opening just one day after MOMI’s Harvey exhibition, famed curator Christiane Paul’s Harold Cohen: AARON at The Whitney Museum’s looked at another seminal media art pioneer.

This author spoke to curator Christiane about the show, which showcased the work of the symbolic AI artmaking program AARON developed by Harold Cohen (1928–2016). Originally conceived in the late 1960s and early 1970s at UC San Diego, AARON was an ongoing experiment in translating artistic knowledge—even an entire practice, a self portrait—into code.

The exhibition featured Cohen’s plotter-generated drawings, painting-machine works and live demonstrations of AARON in action. Positioned against the rise of modern AI tools like DALL-E and Midjourney, the show provided much-needed historical context on AI-driven creativity, authorship and collaboration, emphasizing Cohen’s vision of full machine autonomy in art.

body: The third landmark survey of a new media pioneer at a major global museum in the space of a month, the Centre Pompidou presented Speak to the Eye. Emblematic of an artist gaining recognition too close to passing, the show nonetheless was a welcome celebration of the grande dame of generative art, perhaps our most venerated figure—Vera Molnár.

The show spanned the legend’s career from early hand-drawn geometric abstractions—her machine imaginaire—to her sustained and forever-important serial algorithmic compositions. The show did well at demonstrating Molnár’s systematic emphasis—how she explored ideas and of form, order and controlled randomness throughout her life. It was obssession that would have resulted in a complete and storied practice with or without the computer. But the computer was the artist’s superpower and one of the loves of her life.
The exhibition even examined Molnár’s late experiments with AI-generated art, which she revealed to aurèce vettier.
The show at France’s preeminent modern art institution was a show befitting the career of an all-time great, not only in French, generative or digital art.
To mark the occasion, I wrote about “Molnár’s Paris.”
