body: February 22nd in Paris marked the launch of Taschen’s On NFTs, an early major art historical survey of the NFT ecosystem, authored by artist and researcher Robert Alice. The book features academic essays and richly illustrated profiles of 101 key artists—many of whom were in Paris for the week—connecting NFTs to broader art history and positioning the medium within a lineage of algorithmic, conceptual and digital art. The launch came during a busy and memorable week in Parisian digital art history, which also witnessed Bright Moments and NFT Paris, with the Vera Molnár show opening at the Pompidou the following week.

Also in February, electronic musician and digital artist Agoria brought Le Code d’Orsay to the Musée d’Orsay in a surreal convergence of one of the world’s great, historic collections, contemporary generative art, blockchains and biology. The exhibition also featured Σ Lumina, an interactive steel sculpture co-created with Johan Lescure, which produced shadows in the shape of scannable QR codes. These codes could then be used to mint an NFT on fxhash using the Tezos blockchain. Delightfully, the work incorporated visitors’ breaths to alter the visual composition in real time. If a world-class-museum-worthy work of art wasn’t enough, Agoria also composed an original tribute to the museum, which he performed during a DJ set in its historic nave amongst ancient statues.

In its second-to-last stop on its global tour, Bright Moments brought its traveling community and immersive minting and art experience to NFT Paris, transforming a café into a hub for generative and AI-based art, organized by artist Emily Edelman.

This iteration of Bright Moments would be the last to feature new artist live minting projects. Standouts included Lauren Lee McCarthy’s Seeing Voices and Linda Dounia’s Flore Perdue. I spoke to both artists about the projects leading up to the event.

This online blockchain-based exhibition by MoMA and Feral File brought together seven artists to explore the intersections of sound, technology and art. Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst’s Play from Memory examined human and machine learning in music, while Yoko Ono’s SOUND PIECE V (1996/2024) created an on-chain archive of laughter.
Danielle Brathwaite-Shirley’s CANCEL YOURSELF (2024) reimagined agency through an interactive soundscape and 0xDEAFBEEF’s PAYPHONE (2024) explored telephony and tokenization.

Honoring MoMA’s legacy of sound art, extending to great curators like Barbara London, the exhibition showcased how new technologies—from generative AI to blockchains—can reimagine auditory experience.

body: In March, Artforum announced art historian, curator, and longtime contributor Tina Rivers Ryan as its new Editor in Chief. Ryan, known for her expertise in digital and video art, served as curator at the Buffalo AKG. Ryan closed the year and her time at the reopened Buffalo AKG with the fantastic Electric Op.
The move was a major step forward for digital art, as one of its biggest proponents now heads one of its most renowned publications.

body: The 2024 Whitney Biennial took on the topic of AI, without actually fully committing to its investigation. It did, however, include Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst’s xhairymutantx, an interactive piece built around a generative model that investigates themes of identity, digital presence and the malleability of training data. Presented both in the museum’s sixth-floor gallery and online via artport, the project manipulates Herndon’s visual likeness. Viewers are able to distort her recognizable red hair and features through AI-generated transformations dictated by prompting. The work subverts traditional text-to-image models by limiting the viewer to the world of the artist’s creation rather than the generalities of a generic deep generative model. It was interactive and gave users permission to enjoy using generative AI—many perhaps for the first time.

body: At the end of April, during the opening of the Venice Biennale, Bright Moments concluded its three-year global journey. To mark the occasion, it organized and released the Finale Collection, a unique generative art project uniting over sixty artists on a single contract.

This final act celebrates community, transformation, and reflection, encapsulating the project’s evolution across nine cities. The collection, minted on a single contract, mirrors Bright Moments’ ethos—blending digital and physical, randomness and curation—as it brings together pioneering artists and collectors one last time.

Beyond the collection was the actual event, Bright Moments Venice itself. Taking place in a 14th-century scuola architectural complex over three days, the event brought out mixed emotions as it was simultaneously a celebration and a farewell as the organization reached its final destination with an unclear future. Befitting the local, the event included a Bright Moments documentary as well.

Beyond the Biennale and Bright Moments, there were several other relevant exhibitions at the same time, including Christoph Büchel’s Monte di Pietà, Memo Akten’s Boundaries, Huemin and Ganbrood’s The Dream Cathedral and Sam Spratt’s The Monument Game.

Le Random co-organized a day of talks that included this author interviewing Analívia Cordeiro live and thefunnyguys giving the keynote address. The “mile” consisted of two venues within a fifteen-minute walk of the Art Basel venue proper. First was space25, a three-story space curated by AI gallerists Fellowship. body: Early July saw a third major European summer digital art event and this was the most spectacular and historic. Organized by Dr. Susanne Paech from the HWF Foundation and held at Akademie der Künste in Berlin, The Generative Art Summit Berlin was a once-in-a-lifetime event. It brought together nearly every living historical pioneer able to travel, including Frieder Nake, Larry Cuba and Joan Truckenbrod.
This author and thefunnyguys were interviewed by Dr. Paech, demonstrating the Summit’s willingness to embrace the new.

It explored generative art’s various faces across decades, from early analog experiments to AI-driven creativity. Hosted by the Foundation Herbert W. Franke, himself a critical figure, the show brought together past and present in a way that may be impossible to achieve again in the future. It was a special week in Berlin.

In September, Getty’s PST ART: Art & Science Collide began, exploring art and science through 50+ exhibitions, public programs and research initiatives across Southern California. This included at UCLA, where artists Lauren Lee McCarthy and Casey Reas, along with Chandler McWilliams, presented an exhibition and a research project as part of the program, which I got to speak to them about.

I also spoke to Getty Research Institute’s Nancy Perloff about another show as part of the program, Sensing the Future: Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.). Listen here (transcript) or on your favorite podcast platform.

Finally, the later-discussed Digital Witness at LACMA was also part of the broader Getty PST ART, which is why Tina Rivers Ryan mentioned it when describing the “moment” digital art had at the end of 2024.

body: In September, easily one of 2024’s most important shows opened: Radical Software: Women, Art & Computing 1960–1991. Curated by Michelle Cotton, the show surveyed the history of digital art from a feminist perspective, highlighting women pioneers in computational art’s history. The exhibition also uncovered and/or brought to the fore much vital research, as evidenced by the diversity of the show. It featured over 100 works by 50 artists from fourteen countries and spanned from 1960s–1991, covering early mainframe experiments to the rise of personal computing. It emphasized how artists often collaborated with scientists and engineers to create the newest digital works across drawing, film, performance and text. Positioned within the second wave of feminism, the exhibition challenges conventional tech-art narratives, celebrating women’s overlooked contributions to digital creativity before the internet’s public emergence. For this and many other reasons, Tina Rivers Ryan mentioned this specifically to me as key to digital art’s “moment” at the end of 2024.

body: In September, one of the most important shows of the year opened with Electric Op. Six years in the making, according to curator Tina Rivers Ryan, the show examines how Op art, video, and digital media evolved together, shaping the way images are created and perceived. The show demonstrates the historical genealogy of digital art, building on previous attempts by curators such as Margit Rosen’s bit international at ZKM in 2008.

Featuring more than 100 works by nearly ninety artists from the past six decades, the exhibition explored how artists use of geometric abstraction and optical illusions led directly to engagement with new technologies, like the computer.

What’s daring about the show is that it brings the story to the present, when most historical surveys end around 1990. By showcasing how contemporary artists like LoVid carry forward the legacy of Op art, the exhibition demonstrates its resonance with the present and past.

Electric Op juxtaposes contemporary digital art luminaries such as Cory Arcangel and Rafael Lozano-Hemmer with historical figures like Bridget Riley and Vera Molnar, repositioning Op art as a key movement in the Information Age—if not the first as Ryan argues.

I spoke to four of the exhibiting artists at Electric Op, including Arcangel and Lozano-Hemmer. They reflect on their unique practices and contributions to the show. Another example of the “moment” digital art had at the end of 2024.

img.cap: An installation view of the exhibition, not a single work: a gallery hung with a large orange monochrome, two small Op prints and a pixelated colour-block painting, with a heaped stack of obsolete televisions, monitors and screens massed on the floor at the centre.
img.credit: Installation view of Electric Op, Buffalo AKG Art Museum, 2024. Photo: Brenda Bieger, Buffalo AKG Art Museum.

body: In October, digital art continued its strong autumn with this author’s work of the year, The Call at Serpentine by Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst. Berlin-based duo Herndon and Dryhurst collaborated with Serpentine Arts Technologies to present The Call, an immersive installation exploring AI as a tool for collective creativity. The show serves as a moving example of what Dryhurst has described as protocol art, where the work’s emphasis lies in its underlying systems of coordination, governance and interaction rather than a single static output. Inspired by choral traditions, the project develops new protocols for training AI, incorporating recordings from fifteen UK community choirs. The installation unfolds across three thematic spaces, each reflecting key aspects of AI: compute, data, and model. The Hearth—a striking organ-like instrument powered by GPU fans—symbolizes computation, filling the space with hymns generated by AI. The Wheel presents spatialized recordings of participating choirs, referencing ancient religious structures while reflecting contemporary data collection practices. In The Oratory, visitors actively engage, singing into a microphone that triggers an AI-generated choral response, mirroring the participatory nature of both collective singing and AI training. By reframing AI as a communal rather than individual process, The Call examines data ownership, artistic authorship and the potential for AI to function as a shared cultural and technological language. The show clearly belongs with digital art’s 2024 fall “moment.”

img.credit: Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst, The Call (The Hearth), 2024. Courtesy of the artists and Serpentine. Photo by the author

body: October was a big month for digital art, especially in London. In addition to Serpentine’s The Call, October included the Victoria and Albert Museum’s (V&A) inaugural Digital Art Season to partly coincide with Frieze London as well.

Included in the V&A’s programming was the launch of the museum’s new historical digital art book, Digital Art: 1960s to Now, edited by curators Melanie Lenz, Corinna Gardner and Pita Arreola. I was able to attend this launch along with wonderful talks by Arreola and artist Kyle McDonald.

The following day at the V&A was FEMG3N, the third installment of FEMGEN, featuring a discussion with artists Licia He and Anna Ridler, writer Charlotte Kent and curator Melanie Lenz, alongside a talk by myself on the contributions of women in generative art. I highlighted Eudice Feder and Joan Shogren for their barely-known contributions and wonderful stories.
Founded in 2022 by Micol Apruzzese and Alex Estorick, FEMGEN fosters inclusivity in digital art, celebrating female and nonbinary artists working with generative systems.
The V&A also showed a screening of Gary Hustwit’s generative documentary Eno on legendary musician Brian Eno.

Besides Frieze London and all of its ancillary events, October in London also saw the Lumen Prize 2024 Awards Presentation. It was a busy month for digital art in one of its world capitals and clearly part of 2024’s digital art “moment.”

In October during Frieze London, it’s notable to point out that the fair’s main award went to an AI artist in 2024, Lawrence Lek. For winning the award, Lek debuted Guanyin: Confessions of a Former Carebot, a multimedia installation blending AI and Buddhist mythology.
This author spoke to Lek about his unique, narrative AI films, which barely—or don’t—incorporate the technology at all but asks some of the most evocative questions on the subject.

body: A busy October for digital art ended with a small digital art event in Yamaguchi, Japan, showcasing how this 2024 was not restricted to Europe and the United States; this was a global movement. Held at the wonderful Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM), which was featured previously on this Timeline as a major moment in Japanese digital art history when the facility opened in 2003.

I was fortunate to be invited to speak at the event, organized by Shunsuke Takawo, called InterLab Camp vol.5: Homo Codens—How Will Humanity Draw in the AI Era? It was an intensive workshop that explored generative art, AI-assisted creativity and how coding as an expressive tool continues to expand. Participants came from all walks of life and participated in hands-on sessions, discussions and collaborative projects.
It showed the passionate roots of creative coding, where market forces and “floor prices” were the last things on anyone’s minds.

body: At the end of November, another event in Getty’s PST ART opened, perhaps the most significant—Digital Witness: Revolutions in Design, Photography, and Film. The show is the successor show to LACMA’s 2023 Coded: Art Enters the Computer Age, 1952–1982. Digital Witness picks up essentially where Coded left off, exploring the previous four decades of digital image manipulation and tracing its impact on photography, graphic design and visual effects. Featuring over 150 works by nearly 200 creators, the exhibition examines technology’s impact on digital aesthetics, realism and storytelling, highlighting the accessibility and influence of editing tools today. In this sense, the show is less about generativity per se but is still an important exhibition of digital art’s history. Tina Rivers Ryan mentioned the show specifically when referring to the end of 2024 and its “moment” for digital art.

body: If Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst’s The Call is my work of the year. The exhibition of the year is Tate’s Electric Dreams.

The show at Tate Modern is a major exhibition celebrating the early pioneers of optical, kinetic, programmed and digital art from the 1950s and Japan’s Gutai to the dawn of the internet age. What’s striking about the show is it’s Tate’s—one of the world’s most visited museums'—first focus on digital art since Tate Modern opened twenty-four years earlier, in 2000. In other words, this is a big moment for digital art.

I had the pleasure of speaking to the show’s curator, Val Ravaglia, who curated it with Odessa Warren and Kira Wainstein, twice about the show. First, in a written piece where we discuss historic challenges to artist’s working with technology and much more. Then in Part 2, a video interview, we some of the specific curatorial concerns of the show, especially display.
I also interviewed three legendary exhibiting artists from the show: Rebecca Allen, Analívia Cordeiro and Eduardo Kac, who exemplify the aims of the show. Yes, I thought the show was important.

More about this landmark show. It brings together over 150 works by more than 70 artists from across Asia, Europe and the Americas, showcasing the geographic diversity of digital art’s roots. It explores how artists intervened with emerging technologies in various ways to create immersive environments with just optical illusions, interactive installations and machine-generated imagery. These innovators experimented with light, motion and perception, responding to the increasing presence of technology in daily life. While touching on similar roots to Buffalo AKG’s and Tina Rivers Ryan’s Electric Op, Electric Dreams has a broader focus and incorporates more of digital art’s twentieth-century roots.

For example, the exhibition highlights key artistic movements and moments going back to Gutai, ZERO, New Tendencies and a special section dedicated to Jasia Reichardt’s, of course, legendary Cybernetic Serendipity. Of particular focus for Ravaglia was showcasing how artists reclaimed machines from military and corporate contexts to explore new creative possibilities. Works range from early experiments with video synthesizers like the Sandin Image Processor and algorithmic art to psychedelic environments and home computer-generated imagery.

Importantly, the show juxtaposes historical analog artists including Atsuko Tanaka, Otto Piene and Julio Le Parc with pioneering digital practitioners like Nam June Paik, Harold Cohen, Rebecca Allen and Suzanne Treister.
Electric Dreams was a major museum’s historical retrospective on digital art and its roots—exactly the kind of dialogue with the public that digital art needs to be having moving forward.

body: Among the final moments of 2024 is another of the world’s great museums and perhaps the most renowned modern art institution showcasing generative algorithms on its giant Garden Lobby screen with Light: Rafaël Rozendaal.
I spoke to Rozendaal about the opportunity and his illustrious career.

Known for treating code like paint, Rozendaal transforms the browser—and MoMA’s 25-foot screen—into a fluid canvas. His minimalist animations, designed to be accessible to anyone, anywhere, embody lightness in both concept and execution, with each piece occupying mere kilobytes. The exhibition highlights Rozendaal’s pioneering approach to generative art, emphasizing resolution-independent, future-proof works. By immersing viewers in shifting colors and forms, Light offers a digital meditation in a world of increasing complexity.

body: You can sum up 2025 in two words: vibe coding. There. Timeline 2025 finished.

But wait. That’s not all. The concept captures more than at first glance: the rise of AI agents, Opus 4.5, AI autonomy, new directions in art, new directions for humanity. It’s an examination of how deep learning AI technologies continue to impact our lives, culture and art on practically a turn-by-turn basis. It also raises questions about autonomy, AGI, ethics, consciousness and what is even possible with computation now that we—anyone, you, me—can mold it like never before.
We’ve all been given Pandora’s black box. For the creative potential alone, that’s at least exciting.
[[Le Random asked twelve trusted artists, curators and collectors to choose the single artwork that mattered most to them in 2025.] ](lerandom.art)
Another major development of the year is how AI agents are pointing to the most exciting future direction in art: worlds, living protocols and symbients. I’ll explain.

Last year and bleeding into the beginning of 2025, we saw protocol art come into prominence as a coherent, articulated idea, even though the term has been around for decades. This idea was exemplified by Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst’s The Call from late 2024 as well as World Computer Sculpture Garden curated by Oxfff.

Early 2025 then brought PXL DEX by Kim Asendorf, Cycles by Material Protocol Arts and Infinite Garden by Leander Herzog. A more precise label for much of this work—while it still sits within protocol art—might be smart contract art: systems where code, markets and communities co-produce the artwork over time.

As the year progressed the idea of worlds became more prominent. It became clear that smart contract art was a step (certainly not the final one) in an evolutionary process of increasing complexification in technology in art. Smart contracts were systems and celebrated as such. But they could also be parts of larger systems, cybernetic systems within systems. Smart contract protocols—like those from the end of ‘24 and beginning of ‘25—could now be combined. They sat at the confluence of autonomous deep learning tools, other protocols and autonomous agents, all of which pointed to the development of dynamic, living protocol stacks: worlds.

Worlds are exciting because they tie together so many things, from decades-old artistic inquiries like simulation to the most advanced frontier AI research. Demis Hassabis calls worlds and simulation the thing that interests him most. Other titans obsessed with worlds and AI include Dr. Fei Li (the queen mother herself), Yann LeCun and many others. World Models are the frontier of AI research that emerged in 2025 but are still making their way to public awareness at the start of 2026.

Why are world models so important in AI? Demis Hassabis describes them as a key building block for true AGI. If AI can generate realistic worlds, it likely understands their mechanics. So that’s a thing. Worlds, too, according to Dr. Li, may also be the key to robotics.

So worlds may be the key to AGI and robotics. The implications of those two things in combination have the potential to determine, well, the future of all other intelligences as we know it. So, uh, there’s that. A certain fearlessness is required of the artists most intimately exploring these superpowers.

But before those systems combine to overthrow humanity—or until or instead—worlds are also increasingly essential to understanding contemporary art. Easily some of the most exciting artistic voices are deeply concerned with worlds, from Ayoung Kim and Lu Yang to Ian Cheng, Lawrence Lek, Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst, Primavera De Filippi, Cezar Mocan, dmstfctn, Wendi Yan, terra0 and many more.

What exactly do I mean by “worlds” in this art context? Cheng, in his Emissaries Guide to Worlding, describes them as ”a future you can believe in: one that promises to survive its creator and continue generating drama."
In other words, this is all connected: vibe coding, Opus 4.5, worlds, symbients, the future of art, AGI, robotics, VR/AR, simulation.
Soon anyone can vibe code entire worlds of fantastic weirdness.

Speaking of worlds, in many ways, 2025 was a reality check for the art world, writ large. It was tough for digital and non-digital, blockchain-based and not. But amidst IRL galleries and digital platforms closing left and right, there were signs that the big picture was still intact even if the present was fuzzy. After all, signs of long-term health were just as prevalent: Zero 10, Sasha Stiles at MoMA, Toledo Museum of Art’s Infinite Images and a revitalized digital gallery scene (Yeche Lange, nguyenwahed, HEFT, Offline and more)

Beyond that, 2025 saw a spate of new private digital art spaces funded by some of the field’s most consequential names: Canyon (Robert Rosenkranz), NODE (Micky Malka and Becky Kleiner) and SOLO CSV (Ana Gervás and David Cantolla).
Billionaires are collecting, institutions are here and the art is genuinely as exciting as ever, entering new places as mind-bending as ever.
What were the vibes in 2025? It was a brave new world. And the ones fortunate and curious enough to stay around were handsomely rewarded.

body: The end of January saw one of the year’s strongest projects right off the bat. With PXL DEX, Kim Asendorf extends his experiments with pixels and blockchains by ratcheting up the complexity, treating the pixel as both material and asset.
This author, Peter Bauman, spoke with Asendorf about the work.

PXL DEX comprises 256 “Decks,” abstract 3D animations shown as an isometric matrix of colored points that pulse and warp without looping. Collectors can rotate and zoom each Deck, then tune its visual density by depositing PXL tokens upon purchase.

The work attempts to join ideas of scarcity and perception into linked considerations. By “tokenizing the pixel,” the work could only exist by taking advantage of blockchain-specific affordances. It’s a smart database entangled with cryptoculture, participation and further contestation of art’s objecthood.
Due to PXL DEX’s foregrounding of system mechanics, the work also plays with ideas of protocols in art, as popularized recently by Mat Dryhurst and Holly Herndon plus Primavera De Filippi.
The work was chose by Raoul Pal as his work of the year in our 2025 Favorites article.

body: Another major protocolic art to start the year, Cycles by Material Protocol Arts is a generative artwork on Ethereum, a self-described network sculpture composed of space and time. The project consists of 512 minted “lenses” arranged into rotating rings, forming a continuously shifting 3D kinetic image. Rather than relying on hosted media, Cycles is computed as a live program, rendered on-chain without external dependencies. Each token is a self-contained, perpetually running visual state. Framed as a meditation on recurrence and change, the work uses rotation and depth to unsettle fixed perception. Cycles, along with Kim Asendorf’s PXL DEX (2025) and Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst’s The Call (2024) at Serpentine, all pointed toward the rise of protocol art as a prominent idea at the end of 2024 and beginning of 2025.

body: In late January, DeepSeek released its R1 reasoning model, built on December’s V3. These models shocked the world, as overnight and from seemingly out of nowhere, they matched ChatGPT’s latest benchmarks at a fraction of the price. Markets responded instantly: Nvidia suffered a record one-day market-cap wipeout as investors feared efficiency, not brute-force scaling, could reset AI economics for both the U.S. and China. The releases, called AI’s “Sputnik moment,” invigorated AI as a geopolitical security dilemma, adding an arms-race element to an already combustible situation.

body: In early February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined the term “vibe coding” in a tweet.
The phrase describes a new, casually radical mode of software-making, where the user stops treating code as the primary object and starts treating the interface as the thing you steer.

With LLM-assisted tools (Cursor, voice dictation), the workflow transforms to conversational in natural language as opposed to coding languages. It’s also experimental and opportunistic: “decrease the padding,” accept the change, run it, paste the error, repeat.
The result is the extraordinary ability to direct outcomes with computers, as if they had their own intelligence and agency and weren’t only rigid machines executing explicit binary instructions.

In the first quarter of 2025, AI art moved from a steady undercurrent to a full-on cultural flashpoint. After January’s DeepSeek shock, attention only accelerated when Christie’s staged a high-profile AI-focused sale. The auction drew negative attention from artists all over the world in the form of an anti-AI protest letter, which sharpened the public argument and fears over consent, labour and most of all, replacement. But the auction was also quite successful, totaling $728,784 in sales. Concurrent with this controversy, Verse released p5.js work by Botto, while Keke’s debut on Fellowship signaled growing gallery appetite to spur questions about AI and autonomy. At the same time, Mario Klingemann’s A.I.C.C.A. helped formalize a critical infrastructure around the field. His AI-driven canine critter, er critic, framed the discussion past image-making into interpretation. It treated criticism as a performative, cybernetic system capable of redistributing cultural authority. Together, these signals marked a crescendo where “AI and creativity” became a mainstream art-world storyline. It won’t be the last time this year.

body: July saw undoubtedly one of the year’s most significant events for digital art. Curated by Julia Kaganskiy, Infinite Images: The Art of Algorithms spanned 24 artists from 1961 to the present, framing generativity as a negotiation between chance and control, emergence and intention, authorship and automation. Infinite Images took inspiration, as did Le Random itself, from Vera Molnár’s line: “There is one thing that can replace intuition; it’s randomness.” Four sections move from the “Imaginary Machine” to on-chain long-form, digital materiality and coded nature. The exhibition also served as a sense of validation for a new generation of museum, artist and community. It’s an example of how growth can occur beyond a token or floor price. Sturdier, more sustained growth comes from partnered outreach and showcasing an art form in dialogue with emerging technologies and their impact.

body: June’s impressive Digital Art Mile returned to Basel for a second year. ArtMeta’s Roger Haas and Georg Bak organized the multi-day conference alongside Art Basel, based at Space25 and Kult.Kino, both on side streets between the main fair and the river. The event likely delivered the year’s densest concentration of prestigious panels and speakers.

These sessions addressed the digital art market, museum collecting and infrastructure, corporate and private collections, and generative art and AI. Speakers ranged from Christiane Paul, Hito Steyerl and Regina Harsanyi to Sougwen Chung.

The program combined panels with networking and published recordings of the talks. A dedicated Generative Art and AI day was hosted by Le Random with ArtReview. Le Random’s panel with Sougwen Chung as well as Sofia Crespo and Feileacan McCormick from Entangled Others can be found on YouTube.

body: Also at Basel and easily, easily, easily one of my favorite shows of the year, the most fun, one of the most exciting and with the most durable residence in my head still. The show was a basically flawless demonstration that art can be fun and social as well as relational. It can also be where you least expect it: in the staircases, hidden in small corridors, inside and out. But this isn’t relational, like everyone learns to cook a meal. You want a tattoo? Sauna and cold bath? Give blood? Get your fortune told?

Basel Social Club’s 2025 edition, Bank, repurposed the former Vontobel private bank in Grossbasel into a sprawling, site-specific venue, opening more than 100 rooms to the public. The show worked with the building’s symbolic and material past, as the program used the language of finance and exchange to stage an environment where systems of value became legible as social choreography.

One room in particular, Nina Roehrs’ BANKABLE, presented by none other than a bank, Arab Bank Switzerland, sharpened the show’s finance theme into a direct question of ownership in the digital-cum-blockchain age. It brought together fifteen works linking art, money and value through the lens of decentralized blockchain technology. Artists included Rhea Myers, 0xShiroi, Robert Alice, Mitchell F. Chan, Sarah Friend and Sarah Meyohas.

But just step outside that room and—apparent across the exhibition—across performances and various forms of entertainment (food, bar, music), the bank became a maze of opt-in, novel encounters. It became a place to linger, to queue for (for a long time at some points) and to genuinely not forget.

body: Since March 2023, Beeple Studios in Charleston has developed an ongoing cadence of public-facing shows that treat his practice as a lab for participative experimentation.

That spirit continued into 2025 with evening events that’s blur, like the recently opened NODE and Bright Moments, art with club-like entertainment. It’s part exhibition, performance and social gathering, pulling in both local arts groups and visitors from the crypto scene. In 2025 the schedule included shows like Bitcoin Pizza Day, CryptoPunks Meetup 2.0 and Synthetic Theatre, followed by Charleston Art Night in December.

I spoke with Beeple twice in 2025 and it struck me how the studio’s willingness to experiment with these events is now a crucial part of both his own artistic practice and where I generally see art headed with living, world-like, protocolic systems.

body: 2025 saw New York’s grip as the epicenter of digital art tighten. If the last decades saw the city’s gallery center of gravity shift to Chelsea, then maybe the digital scene is reclaiming the Lower East Side.

On the institutional side, there was excitement, most notably for the announcement of Canyon. The venue opens in 2026 as a “40,000-square-foot contemporary art space devoted to video, sound, performance, and other forms of durational art.”

The gallery scene was more of a mixed bag, due to changing collector habits and an art market scrambling to recalibrate. Okay, bad news first. Words like “burnout” and “old model” were common in describing a rash of gallery shutterings around the world. New York was impacted too with the closings of Venus Over Manhattan and CLEARING, among others. While not a gallery per se, auction house Christie’s also closed its digital art department in September 2025.

Now for the good news: the scene saw the April openings of both HEFT and SuperRare’s Offline. They joined galleries like bitforms, a decades-long stalwart, and the excellent Nguyen Wahed to solidify the Lower East Side as perhaps the global center of permanently displayed digital art. In the neighborhood is also, of course, Rhizome and the newly reopening New Museum to secure the claim. We covered the city’s digital scene in our "New York City Digital Art Guide.”
Also see our New York Art Walk Map.

img.cap: Street view of Nguyen Wahed’s exhibition of Leander Herzog’s Infinite Garden. Courtesy of the gallery

body: Speaking of exciting New York digital-friendly galleries, hello, Galerie Yeche Lange. Located in the Financial District, just below the hotspot in the Lower East Side, the gallery is a physical space for “art on the internet,” with a team including curators Jared Madere, Wretched Worm and Supermetal Bosch; editor Anastasios Karnazes; and developer Miles Peyton.

The space hosted one of 2025’s most impactful shows, One Of Us Is Real And It’s Not You, a group show of artists Supermetal Bosch and Evil Biscuit. Bosch and Biscuit turned the gallery into an “avant NFT” showcase of millennial nostalgia, a collage of the shattered Internet and post-crypto fatigue. There was also a healthy dose of collectible fantasy meeting dissonance with Bosch’s Mons ceramics and chess-like boards shown casually beside Biscuit’s Drifella works.
The show, along with Galerie Yeche Lange’s 2024 opening, signified the wider acceptance of the avant NFT scene, after years of development and a period of self-exile from Ethereum to Solana.

body: If 2025 marked wider acceptance of the avant NFT scene, its culminating statement was Drifella III, Evil Biscuit’s hyper-“schizocollage” project. The work was some of the strongest of the year, to me. So much so that I wrote over 4,000 words about it.

The work from VVV, the digital arm of Galerie Yeche Lange, stands as a high point of art, the Internet and our daily lives in 2025, spanning across 1,333 digital two-dimensional rooms, each presenting a dense triptych. The work turns the derided PFP format into a room-scale composition: painterly layers, meme language, scene lore, and pop-culture fragments, all bursting into an unruly record of the 2020s.

What’s striking about the work is the artist’s comprehension of culture, as Jared Madere put it to me, which is on full display with Drifella III. Built from thousands of traits and references—from painting history to Pokémon to crypto subculture to music to film—Drifella III rewards slow looking. Its sometimes jarring shifts between humor, cringe and the genuine affect while asking what “real” means anyways inside networked identity and masks.
It’s art speaking directly to our Internet-fueled times instead of shying away—even from its unsavory elements—and executed with brilliance by Biscuit.

body: Zero 10 is a case study for our times. It’s clear that 2025–2026 is a transition period for (the world,) the art world and digital art. Art’s digitization went through a whirlwind period of disruptive technologies in successive decades, with deep learning AI and blockchain impacting culture with a one-two blow.

This led to massive shifts in both traditional and digital art worlds, with the ultimate result being a somewhat reluctant integration of what has always been an othered form into more traditional spaces. It began with institutions like MoMA, Tate, LACMA, Pompidou, the Whitney, Buffalo AKG and more.

But the commercial galleries for a variety of complex reasons (client needs, staffing and expertise, education, taste, etc) remained more skeptical and needed to be more conservative as they rely on functioning business models to survive. That means fairs (collections of commercial galleries) would also, even against their will, be more conservative.

Satellite events were tried in Hong Kong from at least 2022 with its Tezos booth quite adjacent—but still separated with a wall and a small door—to the main fair. Then the brilliant Artmeta’s Digital Art Mile in Basel injected much-needed conversation into otherwise uninspiring digital programming. There still wasn’t integration and galleries weren’t going to do it on their own.
What are fairs to do when the most relevant conversations are happening at satellite events? More importantly for them, how do they connect with those buyers?

Perhaps the traditional ways could be subverted. They could carve out a space on the main floor, bypass the traditional gallery selection method and streamline curation directly to people who know the buyers best.

Well, enter Zero 10. It’s a case study for these times in art because it exemplifies its changes. Understand it and its context (how it impacts the digital and traditional galleries forever), and you understand a big chunk of what’s happening. It’s that enormously important.
The show itself debuted at Art Basel Miami Beach in December as the fair’s first dedicated digital art section, curated by Eli Scheinman. This author spoke to Scheinman about the show.

According to Kevin Buist for Le Random, at its strongest, it treated the fair itself as a medium: interactive works, interfaces, responsive systems, and experiments in ownership that couldn’t exist outside networked tools. Beeple’s Regular Animals became the crowd magnet, while projects like Jack Butcher’s Self Checkout and XCOPY’s Coin Laundry foregrounded participation and transparency.

But more importantly than this particular version’s substance, Zero 10 represents quite a shift in the art world’s integration of digital into spaces that mostly held paintings. That messy transition took a big step before our eyes with Zero 10 into a position that’s now more durable and sustainable. Importantly, it’s also far less embarrassing and less new-money show-offy. Zero 10 shows that digital art, after decades, can now be confident and is here to stay.

img.cap: Installation view of Beeple’s Regular Animals with crowd at Art Basel Miami Beach’s Zero 10. Image by Kevin Buist

body: This show and New York’s Museum of Modern Art’s continued support for the digital with their lobby garden screen demonstrate institutional adoption of digital culture at the highest level. Stiles’s A LIVING POEM brings generative language and time-based media to a 24-foot-by-24-foot screen at its entrance for half a year through spring 2026. Stiles envisioned the work as a “poem in residence,” as the piece rewrites and performs itself on an hourly cycle, drawing on Stiles’s original poetry, fragments from MoMA’s text-art collection, custom datasets, p5.js code, GPT-4 and sound. Its multicolored text in Stiles’ familiar palette shifts across fonts, including Cursive Binary, which renders machine code in a handwritten register. An accompanying soundscape by Kris Bones was accessible via QR code, extending the work’s emphasis on sound and liveness.

body: One of my works of the year and one that crystallizes many of my current thoughts about where art is headed (living protocol stacks that form worlds) is Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst’s Starmirror at KW Institute for Contemporary Art, which I discussed with the artists here.

The large-scale installation treats AI as a condition of public space rather than a backstage or blackbox tool. Building on The Call, the project reframed choral participation as a live, opt-in data practice: visitors gather, sing and shape a shared model through ritual and repetition. For the Berlin “chapter,” the duo drew from medieval German repertoire and Hildegard von Bingen, using her canon as training material and a prompt for new collective song.
This author spoke to the artists about the work in 2025.

img.cap: Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst, Starmirror (Installation view with Herndon at KW, Berlin), 2025. Courtesy of the artists and Frank Sperling

body: If anything defined 2025 besides vibe coding, it was change. Institutions were responding to how art itself is changing, becoming more dynamic, interactive, world-like, living, intelligent. That means they needed to become all those too—or build new ones that could be. Enter the major new 2025 venue announcements. In Palo Alto, NODE announced the early 2026 opening of a 12,000-square-foot nonprofit hub for code-based, continuously executing work, built for modular presentation and hands-on learning aimed at bringing new audiences into digital culture. It debuted with 10,000, Matt Hall and John Watkinson’s CryptoPunks exhibition. Meanwhile, across the continent in New York, Canyon was revealed: a 40,000-square-foot space dedicated to video, sound, performance and other durational forms also opening in 2026. Finally, in Madrid, Colección SOLO debuted SOLO CSV, a second venue expanding beyond Espacio SOLO, with new media programs through initiatives like Onkaos. To give you an idea, SOLO in Madrid is the largest, followed by Canyon and NODE. However, NODE is a bit of a different model, intending to be the first of many, while SOLO CSV opened in 2025 and Canyon remained under construction. body: One of the year’s major digital institutional shows, Machine Love at Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum framed the post-pandemic acceleration of AI and virtual life as both medium and subject. The show brought together roughly fifty contemporary works made with game engines, AI and VR, tracking new forms of image-making built from networked datasets, including projects that use generative AI. It was thus a survey on how artists work with datasets and real-time rendering to produce new kinds of images and environments, including avatar-based pieces addressing identity and hyperreal landscape simulations. The show wasn’t a blind celebration of AI though and did take an occasional critical stance. Many works paired immersive installation formats with themes that recur across the current AI debate, involving ethics, ecology, historical interpretation, and questions of life and death. Framed as a cross-section of machine-assisted and machine-collaborative practices, the show positioned these tools as both technical infrastructure and cultural subject matter.

body: Another of the year’s major institutional surveys of AI-driven art, The World Through AI at Paris’s Jeu de Paume, framed artificial intelligence as a split field. It distinguished analytical AI (computer vision, facial recognition) from generative AI, asking how each reshapes our experience of the world. The show brought together around thirty artists working across sculpture, painting, video and installation, with many pieces commissioned or previously unseen, spanning works from 2016 to the present. It opened with a deliberately physical gesture: Julian Charrière’s Metamorphism LI sculptures, cast from artificial lava and melted e-waste, anchoring AI’s supposedly immaterial systems in raw material cost. From there the exhibition moved through projects that mock machine perception, expose the hidden labor underpinning automated platforms, and implicate the viewer directly, as in Hito Steyerl’s installation, where seated visitors become objects available for tagging. The show ultimately wanted to shape how audiences thought about “AI” moving forward. It showed its multifaceted potential, distinguishing generative from analytic, as well as its dangers.

body: With CVPR and NeurIPS, the world’s two most important annual AI conferences, creativity continued to be spotlighted. The main person in the world doing this work at these conferences is Luba Elliott, who covered both events for Le Random. To me, these conferences showcase AI at its most frontier, raw and experimental. It’s the unpolished, more engineering and less art side of AI creativity in all its brilliance.
Elliott’s pieces at Le Random on CVPR and NeurIPS.

At CVPR 2025, curator Elliott’s AI Art Gallery exhibited 70 works in person and 100+ online, positioning computer vision as both research field and image-making substrate. The conversations ranged from Tom White’s interpretability-driven “primary visual concepts” (mapped through Google’s SigLIP) to Justin Urbach’s event-based cameras and Karyn Nakamura’s layered, forensic approach to mediated reality. At NeurIPS 2025, Elliott’s Creative AI Track paired papers and artworks, treating embodiment, interfaces and hybrid agencies as shared research problems.

body: Frieder Nake received the 2025 ACM SIGGRAPH Distinguished Artists Award for Lifetime Achievement in Digital Art, recognizing his foundational role in early computer and algorithmic art in addition to his long influence on computer graphics and digital art.
This author interviewed Nake in July 2024.

One of the foundational figures in computer art, considered one of the three N founders, along with Georg Nees and A. Michael Noll, Frieder Nake is simply a legend. Active since the early 1960s, he was one of the first people ever to intervene with computers artistically. His first computer-generated works date from 1963. He exhibited plotter drawings in Stuttgart in 1965 along with Nees in one of the world’s first digital art exhibitions.

His work appeared in landmark exhibitions including Cybernetic Serendipity (ICA London) and Tendencies 4 (Zagreb), along with many others since, like LACMA’s Coded and Tate’s Electric Dreams. Beyond this major institutional recognition, his work also resonates in 2025 as the history of cybernetics and deep learning AI is more closely recognized. Nake was influenced in Stuttgart by Max Bense’s information aesthetics, shaped by cybernetics and information theory. In 2024, this author interviewed Nake at Le Random, where the artist framed algorithmic art as live, changing systems rather than static outputs.
This explains the importance of Nake. He was one of the first to understand this and he holds today the key to new forms of art that will only continue to increase in relevance: living, dynamic art.

body: “A living work of art,” Autonomous Forest frames ecological stewardship as a techno-legal artwork. A decade in the making, the work by artists Paul Kolling and Paul Seidler stands as one of the clearest examples of a living protocol world, as discussed in moments throughout this year including the first.
This author spoke to the artists about “terra0’s evolution over the last 10 years.
The project pairs a German association (Verein) with a DAO to collectively acquire and hold forest land, then govern it through voting mechanisms on the blockchain.

Emerging from terra0’s 2016 white paper by Paul Seidler, Paul Kolling and Max Hampshire and later experiments like Flower Tokens and Primna Demon, the project developed into a practical structure designed to remove ecosystems from profit-driven extraction and allow regeneration on its own terms.

The end of 2025 saw the project’s NFT launch, which marked a further surrender of artistic control. Its proceeds will fund the acquisition of a third forest plot and the next phase focused on building a community capable of steering the work long-term.

body: The show of the year for me was Room Service, Glitch Residency’s collaborative, sprawling, relational, all-night culmination in a Burgundy chateau. After two weeks of talks, making, workshops and late-night discussions, roughly fifty residents turned the French castle into a maze of opt-in encounters: projections on the façade, improvised rituals, sound baths, interactive games and pop-up “rooms.” It’s part relational installation, performance and part Rirkrit Tiravanija-hosted cybernetic Eyes Wide Shut-themed party. At the same time, it was AI and tech centered in the way I love: weird, uncanny, only possible now. It had the looseness of a salon but it was tied together as a cybernetic system, creating a feedback loop of art, technology and behavior. It was a micro-world in an evening, the kind of experience art will be increasingly exploring into 2026.

body: If nothing dominated 2025 like vibe coding, then the art of the year should be…Claude Opus 4.5. Computation has changed with Anthropic’s Claude Opus and “vibe coding.” What was previously only possible with years of coding knowledge or a developer can now be accomplished in minutes—assuming you’ve paid for enough tokens—in natural language. The magnitude of Claude really hit me at Glitch Residency, where vibe coding was the air everyone breathed at the chateau; it was everywhere, on every laptop, on every lip, a part of every discussion. Is it that some used ChatGPT while others used Gemini? No. Every serious (and non-serious) coder in the room used Claude Opus; it was remarkable. This is what artists do. They constantly test new tools to see how they can express themselves more clearly. AI is the most powerful tool humanity has built, and it’s the same for artists. It opens up seemingly unlimited creative opportunities to bend and sculpt computation in ways that illuminate our society, its promise, its challenges, and this landed alien civilization we’re somehow creating.

body: Contemporary scholarly work on AI is always welcome. Enter Gary Hall, a professor of media at Coventry University and co-founder of Open Humanities Press, who published Masked Media: What It Means to Be Human in the Age of Artificial Creative Intelligence in 2025. As the subtitle says, the book asks what human creativity and authorship mean once machines generate text and images, a question Hall had long pursued as an advocate of open access and experimental forms of scholarly publishing.
